**Summary.** This paper introduces Dissipative Quantum Reservoir Computing (DQRC) as a method to create digital twins for complex quantum systems. By using a small, fixed open quantum system as a reservoir, it learns the input-output map of difficult dynamics, such as High-Harmonic Generation. The results show this approach is highly accurate and generalizes robustly across varying physical driving conditions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work bridges the gap between complex, non-equilibrium quantum dynamics (like HHG) and modern machine learning techniques, proposing a physically constrained, data-driven modeling tool that respects underlying physical principles.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Modeling the complex, nonlinear, and history-dependent input-output dynamics of driven many-body quantum systems from raw data is computationally prohibitive.

**Main result.** A Dissipative Quantum Reservoir Computing (DQRC) framework successfully acts as a compact, physically grounded digital twin, reproducing complex quantum dynamics like High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) using a minimal, fixed quantum reservoir.

**Method.** The authors propose using a DQRC, which trains only a classical readout layer while the reservoir dynamics are governed by a fixed, dissipative quantum evolution (Lindblad master equation).

**Model / system.** The framework is tested on simulating the input-output mapping of a driven many-body system, exemplified by the High-Harmonic Generation (HHG) process in a medium, and benchmarked against a ten-spin Ising chain.

**Key observables.** Reconstruction accuracy ($	ext{R}^2$ score) and amplitude-aware permutation entropy ($	ext{H}_{	ext{amp}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Drive amplitude ($F_0$), driving frequency ($\omega$), and the reservoir size (minimal single-qubit reservoir).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The study assumes that the essential physics can be captured by mapping the dynamics onto a minimal, fixed, dissipative quantum reservoir, rather than requiring a full simulation of the microscopic Hamiltonian.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the input-output problem ($\vec{E}(t) ightarrow 	ext{Medium} ightarrow \vec{Y}(t)$) and show the amplitude dependence of the entropy ($	ext{H}_{	ext{amp}}$) for the reservoir's generalization capability.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the difficulty of modeling quantum dynamics, introduces the DQRC framework by drawing parallels to classical reservoir computing, details the physical implementation using dissipative quantum dynamics, and finally validates the model's generalization capability across varying drive strengths.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Modeling the response of driven many-body quantum systems from input--output data is difficult: the dynamics are nonlinear, history dependent, and expensive to simulate as system size grows. A paradigmatic case is High-Harmonic Generation~(HHG), where a strong field drives a medium to emit radiation that is highly sensitive to the drive and encodes long-range temporal correlations. We introduce a dissipative quantum reservoir computing~(DQRC) framework that builds a digital twin of such a system, learning its input--output map directly from data while the reservoir---itself a small open quantum system---stays fixed and only a classical readout is trained. We show that a minimal single-qubit reservoir reproduces the HHG response of a substantially larger Ising spin chain, and on a representative benchmark matches and on several metrics surpasses previously reported temporal convolutional and Kolmogorov--Arnold-network models, while using a simpler, physically realizable system. A single fixed reservoir further generalizes across a broad range of drives, indicating that it learns a shared physical response structure rather than memorizing trajectories. These results establish dissipative quantum reservoirs as compact, physically grounded digital twins for nonlinear, memory-dependent quantum dynamics.   Code is available at \href{https://github.com/AI-and-Quantum-Computing/DQuRC}{https://github.com/AI-and-Quantum-Computing/DQuRC}.

</details>

### ⭐ [Deciding the Attainability of the Multiparameter Quantum Fisher Information is NP-Hard](http://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35975v1)

**Highlighted author(s):** Alexey V. Gorshkov  
**Authors:** Lorcan O. Conlon, Laura Shou, V Vijendran, Kishor Bharti, Aritra Das, Simon K. Yung, Jacob M. Taylor, Alexey V. Gorshkov, Jun Suzuki, Syed M. Assad  
**Type:** theory · **Category:** quantum information and computing · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.35975v1>  
**Analysis basis:** full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
**Topic relevance:** `quantum measurements` **3/5**

<div class="figure-strip-hint">↔ Scroll figures horizontally</div>
<div class="paper-figures-scroll">
<figure class="paper-figure-card">
<img src="2609.35975_figures/2609.35975_fig1.jpg" alt="Figure 1">
<figcaption class="paper-figure-caption"><b>Fig 1.</b> FIG. 1: Schematic depiction of main results. The left and right outer blue ovals denote the set of all matri- ces Y of a certain dimension and the corresponding set of multiparameter estimation problems defined in Theorem 3 respectively. In this work, we map the problem of deciding whether a given matrix Y is separable or not to the problem of deciding whether the QCRB is attainable (Theorem 3). As it is known that deciding whether a bipartite density matrix is separable or not is NP-hard (Theorem 2), this im- plies that deciding whether the QCRB is attainable or not is also NP-hard (Theorem 4).</figcaption>
</figure>
</div>

**Summary.** This paper proves that determining if the theoretical precision limit set by the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) is actually achievable in quantum parameter estimation is an NP-hard problem. By reducing the problem to the known hard problem of matrix separability, the authors show that a general, efficient criterion for QFI attainability cannot exist unless P=NP.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep theoretical constraint on quantum metrology, showing that even calculating the best possible precision bound (QFI) does not guarantee that the bound is physically achievable without solving an NP-hard problem.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the fundamental question of determining whether the precision limit set by the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) for estimating multiple parameters is actually attainable using individual measurements on a quantum state.

**Main result.** They prove that deciding QFI attainability is NP-hard, establishing a fundamental computational barrier: unless P=NP, no efficient general criterion for attainability can exist.

**Method.** The proof relies on a polynomial-time reduction from the known NP-hard problem of determining the separability of a bipartite density matrix to the QFI attainability decision problem.

**Model / system.** The analysis concerns quantum parameter estimation in a general quantum state $\rho(\theta_1, \dots, \theta_p)$ within a $D$-dimensional Hilbert space, utilizing the framework of Symmetric Logarithmic Derivatives (SLDs).

**Key observables.** The Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) matrix ($J_Q$) and the covariance matrix ($V$) derived from the measurement POVM are the key observables used to test the attainability condition $V = J_Q^{-1}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of parameters ($p$), the dimension of the Hilbert space ($D$), and the structure of the quantum model are important parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that the computational complexity class P $\neq$ NP, which underpins the hardness result. The analysis also considers restricted models like real, constant-rank quantum models.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically maps the NP-hard problem of matrix separability to the problem of QCRB attainability, illustrating the reduction used in the proof.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the QFI bound, frames the attainability as a decision problem, and then constructs a specific quantum encoding model that maps the hard separability problem instance to the QFI attainability question, proving the NP-hardness.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The quantum Fisher information (QFI) sets a fundamental bound on the attainable precision when estimating multiple parameters simultaneously. Incompatibility among the individually optimal measurements can, in some cases, imply that the precision limit set by the QFI is not attainable. In certain special cases, including pure states and full-rank states, the exact conditions for when the precision limit set by the QFI can be saturated are known. However, general conditions for the attainability of the QFI with measurements on individual copies of the quantum state have long been sought. Indeed, this was recently stated as one of the five problems in quantum information theory highlighted by [P. Horodecki et al, PRX Quantum 3, 010101 (2022)]. In this work we prove that exact attainability with individual measurements is NP-hard to decide, even for a restricted set of real, constant-rank quantum models. The source problem for our proof is the NP-hard problem of deciding whether a given bipartite density matrix is separable or not. Our result shows that the longstanding difficulty in obtaining general conditions for QFI attainability reflects a fundamental computational obstruction, rather than merely a limitation of existing mathematical techniques: unless P=NP, no efficiently computable necessary-and-sufficient criterion can exist in general.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors report the first experimental realization of measuring an anomalous weak value using a Bose-Einstein condensate of $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms. By performing a weak Stern-Gerlach measurement and utilizing post-selection, they measured a momentum kick amplified by a factor of 14. This work validates the theoretical framework of weak measurements in an atomic platform, demonstrating its potential for advanced quantum sensing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, state-of-the-art realization of a fundamental quantum measurement concept (weak values) using ultracold atoms, pushing the boundaries of quantum metrology and quantum measurement theory in AMO physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To experimentally realize and measure an anomalous weak value, specifically measuring a component of a particle's spin, as originally proposed by Aharonov et al.

**Main result.** The experiment successfully demonstrated weak value amplification in an atomic system, measuring an effective magnification of a weak magnetic momentum kick by a factor of 14, corresponding to a weak value of 7(3) for $\sigma_z$.

**Method.** A weak Stern-Gerlach measurement was performed on a Bose-Einstein condensate using post-selection on the final state to extract the anomalous weak value.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a Bose-Einstein condensate (BEC) of $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ atoms trapped in a magnetic gradient. The measurement relies on coupling the spin and momentum via a weak magnetic field gradient.

**Key observables.** Pointer shift ($\pi$), weak value ($\langle A angle_w$), and the momentum kick ($\delta_p$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The measurement is sensitive to the momentum kick parameter ($\delta$) and the initial cloud size ($\sigma$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes the initial state is Gaussian for analytical predictions, although the actual atomic cloud profile may deviate.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 shows experimental data comparing the measured momentum shift to weak value predictions for a specific initial size. Figure 3 shows similar results for a larger momentum kick, illustrating the dependence on applied parameters.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory of weak value amplification, details the experimental setup using BECs, presents the measurement of the pointer shift, and compares the results to the theoretical weak value predictions across varying experimental parameters.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The weak value of an operator is the average result of measuring that operator on a quantum system given specified initial and final states. The overlap between these states appears in the denominator of the weak value, and thus if that overlap is small, the weak value can be arbitrarily large. In 1988, Albert, Aharonov, and Vaidman proposed a weak Stern-Gerlach experiment which would be able to measure a so-called anomalous weak value, a measurement result which lies out- side of the eigenvalue spectrum of the operator being measured. Though anomalous weak values have been measured in numerous optical systems, here we present the first such realization of this experiment as originally proposed. By placing a Bose-Einstein condensate of 87Rb in a magnetic gradient and performing an unlikely postselection, we measure an effective magnification of a weak magnetic momentum kick (~ 8 $μ$m/s) by a factor of 14. We also demonstrate that increasing the momentum kick decreases the "weakness" of the measurement and reduces the amplification.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper experimentally demonstrates that a superconducting quantum thermal machine can surpass the precision limits imposed by classical thermodynamics, violating the canonical Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation. By measuring current fluctuations and heat dissipation in a superconducting circuit, the authors show a quantum enhancement in performance at reduced energy cost. This work highlights a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum thermodynamic regimes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a direct, measurable experimental test of fundamental quantum thermodynamic principles, demonstrating a quantum enhancement in precision beyond classical limits, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether quantum mechanics allows for the violation of the classical Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR), which constrains the trade-off between precision and energy cost in non-equilibrium processes.

**Main result.** The authors experimentally demonstrated a violation of the classical TUR in a superconducting quantum thermal machine, measuring a ratio $Q = 1.71 \pm 0.17$, which is below the classical bound of $Q \geq 2$.

**Method.** The experiment uses near-quantum-limited heterodyne detection on a superconducting quantum thermal machine to measure the mean photon current and its fluctuations, allowing for the extraction of the TUR ratio $Q$.

**Model / system.** The system is a superconducting quantum thermal machine built from two flux-tunable transmon qubits forming an artificial molecule, coupled to a cold microwave waveguide bath and driven by classical noise.

**Key observables.** TUR Ratio ($Q$), mean photon current ($J$), and the diffusion coefficient ($D$) extracted from the Power Spectral Density (PSD) of the outgoing microwave field.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The measurement is performed at dilution refrigerator temperatures ($T < 10 	ext{ mK}$); the classical bound is $Q \geq 2$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The classical TUR assumptions (classical Markovian dynamics obeying local detailed balance) are assumed to break down in the quantum regime; the analysis relies on input-output theory and heterodyne detection techniques.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the device architecture, the transport cycle, the PSD of the output field showing emission peaks, and plots showing the measured TUR ratio $Q$ versus drive strength.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the theoretical context of TURs, details the superconducting quantum thermal machine setup, describes the measurement protocol using heterodyne detection to extract current and noise moments, and finally presents the experimental measurement showing the violation of the classical bound.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Precision in nonequilibrium processes comes at a thermodynamic cost: suppressing fluctuations generally requires increased dissipation. Thermodynamic uncertainty relations (TURs) make this trade-off quantitative by linking current fluctuations to entropy production in classical stochastic dynamics. In the decade since its discovery, the canonical steady-state TUR and its finite-time generalizations have become a cornerstone of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, constraining the performance of molecular machines and allowing heat dissipation to be inferred from observable fluctuations. Whether the canonical TUR can be violated in a controlled quantum device remains an outstanding experimental question, in part because doing so requires resolving extremely small steady-state currents as well as their fluctuations. Here we experimentally show that steady-state quantum transport can surpass the precision permitted by the canonical TUR. We observe this violation in a superconducting quantum thermal machine coupled to a microwave waveguide acting as a cold bath and to a classical noise source providing an effective infinite-temperature bath. We observe a TUR ratio $Q = 1.71 \pm 0.17$, in violation of the classical bound $Q \geq 2$. Our results demonstrate a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum thermodynamics, paving the way for quantum thermal devices that achieve enhanced precision at reduced energy cost.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports the realization of single-photon nonlinearity using a quantum dot embedded in a nanobeam cavity. The key innovation is the nanobeam geometry, which allows for high-efficiency coupling to optical fibers while maintaining strong coupling to the quantum emitter. The demonstrated low-threshold nonlinearity establishes this system as a promising, scalable component for quantum photonic circuits.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it combines cavity QED principles (strong coupling, nonlinearity) with practical engineering challenges (fiber coupling, chip integration), providing a robust platform for quantum light sources.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is developing an efficient single-photon nonlinearity for quantum technologies that simultaneously achieves high-efficiency direct fiber coupling and compatibility with scalable on-chip integration.

**Main result.** The researchers successfully demonstrated a single-photon nonlinearity in a nanobeam cavity coupled to a quantum dot, establishing the system as a compact, chip-integrable, and fiber-compatible building block.

**Method.** The nonlinearity was characterized by measuring the cavity reflectivity using weak, resonant picosecond pulses and analyzing the second-order correlation function, $g^{(2)}(0)$.

**Model / system.** The physical system is a quantum dot coupled to a nanobeam cavity, modeled using the Jaynes-Cummings Hamiltonian and analyzed via the Lindblad master equation. The nanobeam geometry facilitates direct coupling to a single-mode fiber.

**Key observables.** Single-photon nonlinearity threshold (0.24 incident photons per pulse), coupling rate ($g/2\pi = 29.1$ GHz), cooperativity ($C = 3.98$), and $g^{(2)}(0)$ measurements.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Fiber coupling efficiency ($\eta_{	ext{coupling}} = 60\%$), cavity decay rate ($\kappa$), and the strong-coupling regime condition ($g > \kappa_1/4$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that linear loss does not alter the underlying photon statistics when calculating $g^{(2)}(0)$ for the integrated system.

**Figures summary.** Figures show the nanobeam design, SEM images, cavity reflectivity spectra exhibiting polariton doublets, and plots detailing reflectivity and $g^{(2)}(0)$ vs. input photon number.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the physical setup, characterizes the cavity and QD coupling parameters using CW light, and then measures the nonlinear response using pulsed excitation to confirm single-photon nonlinearity.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

An efficient single-photon nonlinearity is a key resource for photonic quantum technologies. Single-photon nonlinearities have been demonstrated with quantum dots (QDs) across a range of cavity and waveguide geometries. However, none of these realizations simultaneously provide high-efficiency direct fiber coupling and compatibility with scalable on-chip integration. The nanobeam cavity addresses these limitations through its in-plane geometry, which enables highly efficient, direct fiber coupling alongside scalable homogeneous and heterogeneous on-chip integration. Here, we report a single-photon nonlinearity from a nanobeam cavity coupled to a single quantum dot. The nanobeam interfaces directly with a single-mode fiber with an efficiency of 60%. Driven by resonant picosecond pulses, the platform achieves a single-photon nonlinearity with a low threshold of 0.24 incident photons per pulse. The system operates in the strong-coupling regime, exhibiting a coupling rate of g/2π = 29.1 GHz and a cooperativity of C = 3.98. These results establish the nanobeam cavity-QD system as a compact, chip-integrable, and fiber-compatible building block for scalable photonic quantum technologies.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes adaptive fermion circuits to show that density and coherence localization effects can be tuned independently. By analyzing the system's Liouvillian dynamics, the authors derive separate exponents for density and coherence profiles. This separation is significant because it allows for engineered localization of these two distinct physical properties at opposite ends of the chain.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, controllable platform (adaptive circuits) to study the separation of different types of localization effects (density vs. coherence) in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant to understanding dissipation and measurement backaction in quantum dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** To investigate whether density and coherence skin effects can be independently tuned in adaptive fermion circuits, unlike previous models where they were coupled.

**Main result.** The density skin effect exponent is fixed by measurement strength and feedback displacement, while the coherence exponent can be tuned independently by controlling the relative occupation phase, allowing opposite-edge localization.

**Method.** The analysis uses Liouvillian dynamics, employing gauge transformations and exponential ansatz fitting to extract the decay exponents for both density and coherence profiles.

**Model / system.** The system models spinless fermions on a chain evolving under a trace-preserving Liouvillian governed by measurement-feedback updates, $\partial_t \hat{ho} = \mathcal{L}\hat{ho}$.

**Key observables.** Density skin effect exponent ($\kappa_{	ext{dens}}$), coherence skin effect exponent ($\kappa_{	ext{coh}}$), and the stationary density profile $ho_{n_R}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Measurement strength ($	au$), feedback displacement ($d$), and the relative occupation phase ($	heta$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes an exponential ansatz for the stationary density state and utilizes gauge transformations to map the non-reciprocal dynamics to a normal form for coherence analysis.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the adaptive measurement-feedback update, showing density and coherence profiles at opposite edges, and plot the dependence of $\kappa_{	ext{coh}}$ and $\kappa_{	ext{dens}}$ on control parameters $	au$ and $	heta$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the Liouvillian framework for adaptive circuits, then derives the independent expressions for $\kappa_{	ext{dens}}$ and $\kappa_{	ext{coh}}$, demonstrating their tunability and the mechanism allowing opposite-edge localization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Adaptive circuits use measurements and outcome-conditioned feedback to implement nonreciprocal dynamics without postselection. We show that fermion circuits host independently tunable density and coherence skin effects. The stationary state has an exact density tilt set only by measurement strength and feedback displacement: conditioned-gate details cancel, yielding an exponential one-particle profile and, at any filling, a tilted ensemble of configuration weights. Decaying coherences instead obey, in the bulk, an effective Hatano-Nelson generator controlled by the conditioned gates through a relative occupation phase. Tuning this phase drives a point-gap topological transition and reverses coherence localization at fixed density, allowing density and coherence to localize at opposite edges. We derive both exponents for conditioned $U(2)$ gates and propose a correlator-ratio probe using ensemble-averaged observables.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper analyzes how work fluctuations scale when a quantum system is driven through a time-dependent process, comparing predictions from the Kibble-Zurek mechanism (critical dynamics) against those from Adiabatic Perturbation Theory (smooth driving). By solving the problem for a Gaussian field theory, the authors map out the precise crossover scaling laws governing the excess-work cumulants. This work provides a foundational, solvable model for understanding non-equilibrium thermodynamics in complex quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit derivation of crossover scaling laws for work cumulants provides a powerful, solvable model to test general theoretical frameworks concerning non-equilibrium dynamics and critical phenomena in quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the crossover between different scaling behaviors of work cumulants in a driven quantum system, specifically comparing the Kibble-Zurek (KZ) mechanism with the Adiabatic Perturbation Theory (APT) predictions.

**Main result.** The scaling of the excess-work cumulants depends on the relative exponents of the protocol and the dimensionality, exhibiting distinct power-law behaviors, including logarithmic corrections at specific crossover points.

**Method.** The analysis utilizes path integral formulations, mode decomposition, and advanced scaling arguments derived from solving the mode equations for the Gaussian field theory.

**Model / system.** The system is a driven O(N) Gaussian field theory in a d-dimensional box, whose dynamics are governed by a time-dependent Lagrangian density. The analysis focuses on the work cumulants derived from the Characteristic Function of Work (CFW).

**Key observables.** Work cumulants (excess-work cumulants $c_n$), Characteristic Function of Work (CFW), and the Husimi parameter ($Q^*$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Protocol exponent ($p$), spatial dimension ($d$), order of cumulant ($n$), and protocol duration ($	au_Q$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the solvability of the Gaussian field theory and the validity of both the APT and KZ approximations in different regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically derives the CFW for the Gaussian field, first analyzing gapped protocols using APT, and then tackling power-law protocols approaching criticality by comparing the resulting KZ scaling with the regular APT contributions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We derive the finite-temperature characteristic function of work (CFW) for a driven $O(N)$ Gaussian field theory and obtain closed-form expressions for all zero-temperature excess-work cumulants. For gapped protocols, we use adiabatic perturbation theory (APT) to derive the $τ_Q^{-2}$ scaling for protocols with a nonzero first derivative at either boundary, where $τ_Q$ is the protocol duration; smoother boundaries lead to faster decay. For power-law protocols approaching the critical point with exponent $p$, we determine the competition between critical excitations and the regular contribution. The $n$th cumulant's critical contribution follows Kibble--Zurek (KZ) scaling $τ_Q^{-p(d+n)/(p+2)}$ for $d+n<2p+4$, acquires a logarithmic correction $τ_Q^{-2p}\logτ_Q$ at $d+n=2p+4$, and scales as $τ_Q^{-2p}$ above this condition, where $d$ is the spatial dimension. This analytical study of the APT--KZ crossover in a solvable model provides a basis for studying their competition in interacting field theories.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents a near-optimal quantum algorithm to simulate dynamics governed by Lindbladian master equations on a lattice. By utilizing the exact dilation into a system-environment unitary evolution, the authors adapt techniques from Hamiltonian simulation to handle the irreversible nature of open quantum systems. This achieves scaling comparable to state-of-the-art methods, making it highly relevant for quantum simulation of dissipative processes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses simulating open quantum systems (Lindbladians) on quantum hardware, which is a major challenge in quantum computation, by adapting successful techniques from Hamiltonian simulation.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing quantum algorithms to simulate time evolution under geometrically local Lindbladians efficiently.

**Main result.** The authors present a near-optimal algorithm achieving gate depth $O(t 	ext{ polylog}(Nt/\epsilon))$, matching the performance of HHKL for Hamiltonian simulation.

**Method.** The approach involves using an exact dilation of the Lindblad master equation via Quantum Stochastic Calculus and then applying techniques analogous to those used for Hamiltonian simulation.

**Model / system.** The system is a lattice of qudits whose dynamics are governed by a Lindbladian master equation $\mathcal{L} = \sum_e L_e$. The simulation is performed by mapping the Lindbladian evolution to a unitary evolution of an extended system-environment state.

**Key observables.** Approximation error in the diamond norm ($\lVert E - \exp(Lt) Vert_\diamond \le \epsilon$), and the required gate complexity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Evolution time ($t$), system size ($N$), and approximation error ($\epsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis requires bounding the environment state to a low-excitation subspace and relies on constructing efficient block-encodings for the system-environment dynamics.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the dilation of the Lindblad evolution, showing how jump operators couple the system to independent bosonic fields, and how the system-environment interaction is modeled.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem using the Lindbladian and its dilation. It then develops techniques to bound the system-environment interaction within a low-excitation space, culminating in the construction of unitaries using block-encoding and polar factor approximations to achieve the final complexity bounds.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We consider the problem of simulating dynamics under geometrically local Lindbladians acting on a lattice of qudits. We present an algorithm to approximate the time evolution under these Lindbladians for evolution time $t$ and on $N$ qudits to diamond norm error $\varepsilon$ using geometrically local circuits of depth $O(t \ \polylog(Nt/\varepsilon))$. Our results thus achieve a performance comparable to that of the Haah-Hastings-Kothari-Low (HHKL) algorithm for lattice Hamiltonian simulation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates a novel method to dynamically control and tune diamond photonic cavities using only light. By inducing both fast thermal shifts and slow, quasi-permanent charge-mediated blue-shifts, the authors establish a highly reconfigurable platform. This work is crucial for developing integrated quantum and nonlinear photonic technologies.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work directly addresses the integration of quantum emitters (NV centers) into advanced photonic circuits, providing a platform for quantum light sources and nonlinear optics, which is central to quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is developing practical, dynamic, and tunable mechanisms for controlling monolithic diamond photonic circuits.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated all-optical modulation ($\approx 45\%$ depth) and long-lived, reversible tuning ($\Delta\lambda = 3.15 	ext{ nm}$) of diamond photonic cavities using green light excitation.

**Method.** The study employed optical spectroscopy, using an IR laser to probe the cavity resonance while modulating or illuminating it with a green laser (532 nm) to induce changes.

**Model / system.** The platform utilizes suspended diamond Fabry-Perot nanobeam cavities containing Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) color centers. The physics involves competing contributions to the cavity shift: a thermo-optic red-shift and a novel charge-mediated blue-shift via free-carrier plasma dispersion.

**Key observables.** Infrared modulation depth, photo-refractive resonance blue-shift ($\Delta\lambda$), cavity linewidth, and time-dependent resonance shifts.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Modulation depth of $\approx 45\%$; maximum tuning of $3.15 	ext{ nm}$ ($0.87 	ext{ THz}$); comparison to high-voltage Pockels modulators.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the free-carrier response is governed by the Drude model and that the observed shifts are due to the combination of thermal and photo-carrier effects.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup, long-lived photorefractive tuning over days, time-domain responses distinguishing fast thermal and slow charge-related shifts, and spectral analysis comparing different illumination conditions.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first demonstrating the feasibility of all-optical modulation and tuning, then analyzing the temporal dynamics to separate thermal and charge-related shifts, and finally performing detailed modeling to confirm the free-carrier mechanism over singlet absorption.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Single-crystal diamond combines exceptional optical, thermal, and mechanical properties while hosting optically addressable and spin-coherent colour centres, making it a promising platform for integrated quantum and nonlinear photonics. However, practical post-fabrication mechanisms for dynamically controlling and tuning monolithic diamond photonic circuits remain limited. Here, we demonstrate all-optical modulation and long-lived tuning of suspended diamond Fabry--Perot nanobeam cavities containing nitrogen-vacancy centres. Under 532~nm illumination, the infrared (1000 to 1100~nm) cavity response is governed by two competing contributions: a well-understood thermo-optic red-shift, and a novel charge-mediated blue-shift that we attribute to the free-carrier plasma dispersion effect. With 10~mW of 20~kHz-modulated green light, we achieve an infrared modulation depth of approximately 45\% of the available reflection contrast. Green illumination also produces quasi-permanent photo-refractive resonance blue-shifts, with a maximum observed tuning of 3.15~nm (0.87~THz), without measurable degradation of the cavity linewidth or contrast. Achieving the same cavity shift in a lithium-niobate Pockels modulator would require 200 to 500~V across a \(5~μ\mathrm{m}\) electrode gap. These results establish a monolithic diamond nanophotonic platform combining agile and reversible modulation with long-lived optical reconfiguration, two key ingredients in photonic technologies.

</details>

**Summary.** This work demonstrates that the mere act of repeatedly measuring and feeding back results from a quantum system can induce collective ordering, even if the system's inherent programmed state is disordered. The ordering transition is controlled by the measurement-feedback interval, leading to dynamics that mimic continuous dephasing models. This highlights the profound role of measurement back-action in shaping macroscopic quantum behavior.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, measurable mechanism (measurement frequency) by which non-equilibrium quantum dynamics can induce macroscopic order, offering insights into measurement-induced phase transitions relevant to open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how the measurement-feedback interval controls the emergence of collective ordering in a quantum Boltzmann sampler, even when the underlying programmed distribution is disordered.

**Main result.** Shortening the measurement-feedback interval drives a continuous transition to an ordered stationary state, and the resulting dynamics map onto those of a continuous dephasing model.

**Method.** The authors derived the exact finite-interval Markov kernel and analyzed the stationary state by comparing discrete measurement dynamics with continuous master equation descriptions.

**Model / system.** The system is a quantum Boltzmann sampler implemented via a partial-reset qubit model, governed by a programmed Hamiltonian and subjected to repeated projective measurements with a feedback interval $\Delta$.

**Key observables.** Invariant polarization ($ar{z}_\Delta(a)$), stationary gain ($G_\Delta$), magnetization ($m$), and critical scaling exponents.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Measurement-feedback interval ($\Delta$), coupling strength ($J_{ij}$), and the environmental dephasing rate ($\gamma=0$ in the main analysis).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes ideal, instantaneous projective measurements and focuses on the zero environmental dephasing rate ($\gamma=0$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate response enhancement exceeding the unmeasured value, the ordering window controlled by the readout interval, and comparisons of linear relaxation rates between the discrete and continuous models.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from deriving the finite-interval Markov kernel and showing response enhancement, to analyzing the continuous transition to order via fixed-point analysis, and finally confirming the differences between the discrete and continuous dynamics through critical scaling checks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that the measurement--feedback interval alone can induce ordering in a quantum Boltzmann sampler with fixed programmed couplings and a fixed local dissipative rule. At zero environmental dephasing, repeated projective measurements remove transverse coherence regenerated during relaxation, thereby enhancing the local longitudinal response. We derive the exact finite-interval Markov kernel for successive measurement records and obtain the ordering threshold in the Curie--Weiss limit. For couplings below the equilibrium Curie--Weiss threshold, shortening the readout interval drives a continuous transition to an ordered stationary state even though the programmed Boltzmann distribution remains disordered. The stationary response and equation of state map exactly onto those of a continuously interacting model with dephasing, while the linear relaxation rates remain distinct at matched static response. Exact finite-size stationary calculations reveal the transition through bimodal magnetization distributions and mean-field critical scaling.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a novel 'asymptotic pseudospectral atlas' to analyze open quantum systems driven by periodic forces, where standard spectral methods fail. By classifying the geometry of the pseudospectra, the authors predict that global structural changes in this atlas correspond directly to measurable physical events, such as the exchange of correlation signal orders in the chiral XY model.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, geometry-based theoretical tool to predict observable changes in complex, non-Hermitian, open quantum systems, linking spectral theory directly to measurable physical phenomena.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the limitations of the Floquet spectrum for periodically driven open quantum systems, necessitating the use of pseudospectra to accurately characterize dynamics in the thermodynamic limit.

**Main result.** The authors establish an 'asymptotic pseudospectral atlas' that provides a geometric structure classifying the validity regimes (exponential, algebraic, bounded) of approximate modes, which dictates observable physical transitions.

**Method.** The core method involves analyzing the asymptotic size-scaling laws of pseudospectral residuals, formalizing this into an atlas that partitions the unit disk into distinct geometric domains.

**Model / system.** The study applies to general periodically driven open quantum systems, demonstrated using specific models like a dissipative shift chain and the chiral XY model.

**Key observables.** Spin-wave observables, correlation signals, and the pseudospectral residual $\epsilon_N(z)$ are used to detect geometric transitions.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key parameters include the driving strength ($g$) and the system size ($N$), which govern the transitions between different scaling regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the 'common-limit hypothesis' for simplifying the asymptotic indices and involves complex block constructions for error bounding.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of the pseudospectral atlas, showing how components merge and holes close at critical parameter values ($g_1, g_2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the pseudospectral problem to introducing the asymptotic atlas, then applies this geometric framework to analyze specific physical models (dissipative shift chain, chiral XY model) to predict observable changes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

In periodically driven open quantum systems, nonnormality renders the Floquet spectrum insufficient as the system approaches the thermodynamic limit, so that pseudospectra are needed to characterize the dynamics accurately. While conventional approaches mainly focus on the local dynamics of isolated pseudospectra, their global connections and the resulting physical consequences for observables have remained largely unexplored. Here, we uncover this collective behavior by classifying the unit disk into distinct domains of exponential, algebraic, and bounded accuracy according to the asymptotic size-scaling laws of pseudospectral residuals, yielding an underlying geometric structure. We demonstrate the physical implications of this structure through two exactly solvable models. First, in a dissipative shift chain, parameter tuning drives geometric transitions that are detectable via spin-wave observables. Second, in a chiral XY model, we use this geometric structure to explain the origin of a measurable phenomenon: two correlation signals exchange their retention order under continuous parameter tuning. Our findings not only establish a new theoretical paradigm for understanding dissipative Floquet quantum systems, but also predict geometry-driven observables for quantum computing experiments.

</details>

**Summary.** This research demonstrates how to use structured light from a spatial mode demultiplexer to exert a radiation pressure force on a mechanical membrane. By mapping the coupling coefficients, the authors show that two-mode illumination can probe spatial derivatives of the mechanical mode shapes. Crucially, they apply this to implement a feedback cooling scheme capable of simultaneously cooling multiple, nearly degenerate mechanical modes.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly bridges quantum optics (structured light, mode coupling) with mechanical quantum systems (nanoresonators, cooling), providing a powerful, scalable tool for quantum state preparation in mechanical oscillators.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper demonstrates the use of multimode radiation pressure to actuate and cool mechanical resonators, overcoming the difficulty of detecting radiation pressure effects with extended objects.

**Main result.** They successfully used two-mode structured light to map spatial derivatives of mechanical mode shapes and achieved selective, simultaneous cooling of two nearly degenerate mechanical modes.

**Method.** The technique involves illuminating a nanomechanical membrane with structured light generated by a spatial mode demultiplexer (SPADE) to exert a radiation pressure force proportional to mode coupling coefficients.

**Model / system.** The system is a $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ nanomechanical membrane resonator. The interaction is governed by the radiation pressure force, which depends on the coupling coefficients $eta_{mn,kl}$ derived from the overlap of optical and mechanical mode profiles.

**Key observables.** Position-dependent intermodal coupling coefficients ($eta_{mn,kl}$), mechanical mode shapes ($\varphi_{ij}$), and the raw displacement power spectral densities (PSDs) showing selective cooling.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The coupling coefficients $eta_{mn,kl}$ are shown to be proportional to spatial derivatives of the mechanical mode shapes, allowing access to higher-order spatial information.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the reflected field approximation for the optical interaction, and the cooling process is modeled using a feedback force proportional to the mechanical velocity ($\propto -\dot{z}$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the setup, showing how single-mode and two-mode illumination maps reproduce squared or derivative forms of the mechanical mode shapes. A key figure shows raw PSDs demonstrating the selective and simultaneous cooling of two distinct mechanical modes.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework for multimode optomechanical scattering and radiation pressure force. It then details the experimental characterization of mode coupling using structured light. Finally, it applies this knowledge to implement a feedback cooling scheme to selectively cool multiple degenerate mechanical modes.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Multimode optomechanical scattering is ubiquitous in free-space imaging protocols, but its radiation pressure counterpart is challenging to detect with extended objects. Here we demonstrate radiation pressure actuation of a nanomechanical membrane using dynamically structured light from a spatial mode demultiplexer (SPADE). Using single- and two-mode illumination, we directly image the position-dependent intermodal coupling between Hermite-Gauss (HG) modes as mediated by the membrane's motion. As an application, we use multimode radiation pressure feedback to simultaneously cool two nearly degenerate membrane modes. Our results are applicable to diverse mechanical systems and serve as a stepping stone to SPADE-based quantum optomechanics.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper explores the deep connection between Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and quantum coherence, demonstrating a factorization law that relates the QFI to the initial state's coherence. By confirming this relationship both theoretically and experimentally using photonic qubits and qutrits, the authors provide a powerful tool for quantum metrology, allowing for parameter estimation bounds based only on initial state properties.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, experimentally verified link between two fundamental quantum resources (coherence and QFI) that govern the ultimate precision limits in quantum sensing, which is highly relevant to quantum optics and quantum information theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the previously unexplored interplay and factorization relationship between the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and quantum coherence in the context of quantum parameter estimation.

**Main result.** The factorization law, linking QFI to the initial state's quantum coherence, is confirmed both theoretically and experimentally for both qubit and qutrit systems. This establishes a lower bound on the parameter estimation variance based solely on initial coherence.

**Method.** The authors employ theoretical derivations for the QFI and coherence measures, which are then verified using experimental measurements on photonic systems.

**Model / system.** The study uses pure states prepared in qubit and qutrit systems, evolving under a unitary transformation $U_{	heta}=e^{-i \hat{H}	heta}$. Experimentally, the platform involves an interferometric network utilizing heralded single-photon sources.

**Key observables.** Quantum Fisher Information ($F_{	heta}$), Quantum Coherence ($\mathcal{C}_{l2}(ho)$), and the variance of the estimated parameter ($	ext{Var}(\hat{	heta})$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The dimensionality of the system ($D=2$ for qubits, $D=3$ for qutrits) and the evolution angle $	heta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the Hamiltonian $\hat{H}$ is independent of the parameter $	heta$ for the simplest QFI form, and the experimental measurements rely on specific unitary operations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the factorization law for QFI vs. coherence in both qubit and qutrit cases, and another figure validates the derived lower bound on the parameter estimation variance.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the theoretical factorization law for QFI and coherence, then presenting the experimental setup and results to verify this law in both 2D and 3D systems, and finally confirming the resulting lower bound on estimation variance.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum Fisher information (QFI) quantifies the sensitivity of a quantum state to a parameter change and plays a key role in quantum metrology. Meanwhile, quantum coherence is a crucial resource for quantum information processing. However, despite extensive studies on various aspects of quantum metrology, the interplay between the dynamics of the QFI and quantum coherence remains unexplored. Here, we explore the factorization relationship between the QFI and quantum coherence, both theoretically and experimentally. We prepare pure states in qubit and qutrit systems and apply unitary evolution to investigate this relationship. Our results confirm the factorization law, offering strong evidence for this relationship. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the variance of the estimated parameter that does not require the final state information. This approach reveals a deep connection between the QFI and quantum coherence, providing insights into quantum parameter estimation. These findings have potential applications in quantum sensing and quantum metrology.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports on observing spin-exchange interactions between circular Rydberg atoms for unprecedentedly long durations (over 60 $\mu$s). The researchers improved the coherence time by an order of magnitude and demonstrated a novel dynamical decoupling sequence. This work paves the way for long-duration quantum simulation of complex, strongly-interacting quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the coherence time limitation in quantum simulation platforms, providing a concrete, experimentally validated method (dynamical decoupling) to extend interaction times for strongly-interacting many-body systems using Rydberg atoms.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge addressed is extending the interaction time for quantum simulations using neutral atoms, as current Rydberg-based systems are limited to microsecond timescales.

**Main result.** The authors observed spin-exchange interactions over timescales exceeding 60 $\mu$s, improving the state-of-the-art by an order of magnitude, and demonstrated a novel dynamical decoupling technique to counteract spin-motion coupling.

**Method.** The study uses laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms to encode spin-1/2 qubits and measures the spin-exchange dynamics by monitoring the population imbalance over extended periods.

**Model / system.** The platform utilizes laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms, forming a hybrid system with auxiliary atoms. The interaction is governed by spin-exchange coupling, and the dynamics are analyzed by measuring the time evolution of the spin coherence.

**Key observables.** Spin-exchange oscillation contrast, population imbalance $M(\delta t)$, and the decay rate of the spin oscillations.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Interaction times exceeding 60 $\mu$s, 40 spin-oscillation periods, and the characteristic decay time $T_1 \approx 59 \mu s$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on post-selection via syndrome measurement to extend the effective qubit lifetime and models the decay due to spin-motion coupling.

**Figures summary.** Figures detail the physical setup, the quantum circuit sequence for state control and measurement, and the measured population imbalance $M(\delta t)$ showing exponential decay of oscillations over time.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the experimental setup, describes the quantum circuit sequence for state preparation and interaction, presents the measurement of the spin-exchange dynamics, and concludes with the demonstration of dynamical decoupling to preserve coherence.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Arrays of neutral atoms excited to Rydberg levels have emerged as one of the most promising platforms for quantum computation and simulation. With the hope to outperform classical devices, the number of atoms has been increased by orders of magnitude. However, the interaction time, i.e., the maximum accumulated time during which an atom interacts with its neighbours, has been limited to a few microseconds only. This restrains the number of gates per atom or prevents the simulation of long-time dynamics of quantum many-body systems. Here, we observe the spin-exchange interaction between two spin 1/2s encoded in laser-trapped circular Rydberg atoms over more than $60μs$ and 40 spin-oscillation periods, improving the state of the art by an order of magnitude. These unprecedented timescales allow us to record for weak atomic trapping a collapse and revival of the spin-exchange oscillation contrast induced by spin-motion coupling. Our results constitute the first observation of this coupling with laser-trapped Rydberg atoms. To counteract its detrimental effect for quantum simulation, we demonstrate a novel dynamical decoupling method that prevents the collapse of the spin oscillations. This method exploits the advantages of our recently developed hybrid platform that enables the measurement and the optical manipulation of long-lived circular Rydberg atoms with auxiliary Rydberg atoms. This work opens a direct route to long-duration quantum simulation of strongly-interacting many-body systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports the successful realization of a single, high-performance quantum light source using a silicon C-center defect coupled to a photonic crystal cavity. By demonstrating strong Purcell enhancement and confirming single-photon emission in the telecom L-band, the research establishes a critical building block for future low-loss quantum communication technologies.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of integrating quantum emitters into silicon photonics, which is a cornerstone technology for scalable quantum networks and quantum communication.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to create a scalable, low-loss, and long-distance quantum light source using single-photon emitters integrated into silicon photonics.

**Main result.** The authors successfully isolated a single silicon C-center and demonstrated single-photon emission ($g^{(2)}(0) = 0.23$) with a significant Purcell enhancement ($F_P \geq 33$) in the telecom L-band.

**Method.** The study combines advanced optical characterization techniques, including time-resolved photoluminescence (PL) measurements and second-order autocorrelation measurements, on a solid-state platform.

**Model / system.** The system utilizes a single C-center defect in Silicon-on-Insulator (SOI) coupled to a high-quality factor nanophotonic crystal cavity. The physics is analyzed using concepts from cavity quantum electrodynamics (Purcell effect) and single-photon statistics.

**Key observables.** Zero-phonon line (ZPL) emission at $\sim 1570$ nm, excited-state lifetime ($	au$), Purcell factor ($F_P$), and the second-order correlation function $g^{(2)}(0)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Telecom L-band (1565 - 1625 nm), Purcell factor lower bound of 33, and $g^{(2)}(0) = 0.23$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the observed enhancement is due to cavity coupling, and the single-photon nature is confirmed by $g^{(2)}(0) < 0.5$.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the PL spectrum vs. detuning, time-resolved PL showing lifetime changes, and the $g^{(2)}(	au)$ measurement confirming single-photon statistics.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical system (C-center in SOI) to demonstrating cavity coupling via PL enhancement, quantifying the enhancement via lifetime measurements (Purcell factor), and finally confirming single-photon emission using $g^{(2)}$ measurements.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Monolithic integration of single-photon sources into silicon photonics offers a compelling solution for realizing scalable quantum telecommunication architectures. Among the candidate silicon color centers, the C-center features a zero-phonon emission in the telecom L-band, corresponding to the spectral window of minimum transmission loss in optical fibers. Despite this advantage, isolating single C-centers has remained an unrealized challenge in solid-state quantum optics. In this work, we report the isolation of a single silicon C-center. We enhance the spontaneous emission rate of the zero-phonon line by coupling the single emitter to a nanophotonic crystal cavity, observing a fivefold reduction in the excited-state lifetime compared to bulk conditions, which corresponds to a Purcell factor lower bound of 33. Second-order autocorrelation measurements confirm single-photon emission from the investigated defect, obtaining an optical purity of $g^{(2)}(0) = 0.23$ without background correction. Our results establish a native telecom L-band quantum light source in silicon, laying the foundation for ultra-low-loss and long-distance quantum applications.

</details>

The absolute relative deviations remain below approximately 0.7% throughout the plotted range.</figcaption>

**Summary.** This paper derives the exact long-time behavior of anomalous spin-current fluctuations in the folded XXZ chain. By mapping the system to the t-0 model and exploiting spin-charge separation, the authors find that the current distribution converges to a non-Gaussian M-Wright function. This provides a rigorous theoretical result for anomalous transport in strongly correlated quantum magnets.

**Why it may be interesting.** The exact derivation of non-Gaussian, anomalous transport statistics in an integrable quantum chain provides deep insights into non-equilibrium dynamics, which is crucial for understanding energy/particle transport in quantum materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the universal aspects of transport in interacting many-body systems, specifically determining the probability distribution of the time-integrated spin current.

**Main result.** The long-time asymptotic distribution of the rescaled time-integrated spin current converges to a non-Gaussian distribution described by the M-Wright function.

**Method.** The analysis involves mapping the folded XXZ chain to the one-dimensional t-0 model, exploiting exact spin-charge separation to reduce the problem to a free-fermion dynamical calculation.

**Model / system.** The study focuses on the folded XXZ chain, which models the strong-anisotropy limit of the XXZ spin chain. The dynamics are analyzed at infinite temperature, utilizing the mapping to the t-0 model.

**Key observables.** The primary observable is the time-integrated spin current, $Q_t$, analyzed via its Moment-Generating Function (MGF), $\langle e^{\lambda Q_t} angle$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The analysis focuses on the long-time limit ($t 	o \infty$) and the scaling of the current, $Q_t/t^{1/4}$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on a nonlocal map to the t-0 model and the assumption that the long-time behavior is governed by the free-fermion dynamics after separation.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares the characteristic function of the current at finite times (t=4, 8, 16) against the derived asymptotic prediction and a Gaussian reference.

**Paper structure.** The paper establishes the problem by defining the MGF for the spin current, derives an exact finite-time expression by mapping to the t-0 model, and concludes with a long-time asymptotic analysis yielding the M-Wright function distribution.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study spin-current fluctuations of the folded XXZ chain, which describes the strong-anisotropy limit of the XXZ chain. We obtain an exact expression for the moment-generating function of the time-integrated spin current at infinite temperature. A long-time asymptotic analysis establishes that the rescaled time-integrated current converges to a non-Gaussian distribution described by the M-Wright function. The derivation relies on a nonlocal map to the one-dimensional t-0 model and its exact spin-charge separation. By extending this approach, we also show that the dynamical correlation function of the spins summed over two adjacent sites exhibits a diffusive Gaussian profile at long times.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates a novel method to generate and measure quantum correlations in attosecond extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) light. By perturbing high-harmonic generation with squeezed vacuum fields, the authors transfer quantum correlations from the infrared to the XUV spectrum. This technique allows for the characterization of quantum dynamics with sub-cycle precision, paving the way for quantum attosecond science.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to AMO and quantum optics as it pushes the measurement of quantum resources (correlations) into the ultrafast, attosecond domain, opening a new frontier for quantum light-matter interaction studies.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is probing quantum correlations between optical modes, ranging from classical fluctuations to quantum entanglement, on the natural timescale of electronic motion—the attosecond regime.

**Main result.** The study successfully establishes a framework for generating and probing quantum correlations on attosecond timescales by mapping correlations from the infrared to the XUV spectrum.

**Method.** The authors use high-harmonic generation (HHG) perturbed by two-mode bright squeezed vacuum (TMBSV) fields, employing even harmonics as an intrinsic, phase-sensitive probe.

**Model / system.** The physical system is the nonlinear interaction in gas-phase HHG, perturbed by a TMBSV field generated via SPDC. The process maps quantum correlations from the IR pump/squeezed vacuum fields onto the broadband XUV harmonics.

**Key observables.** Amplitude correlations (via shot-resolved covariance) and phase correlations (via even harmonics) are measured. Key observables include the joint temporal reconstruction of correlated emission and the mean harmonic response vs. delay.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The measurement operates in the attosecond regime, utilizing the transfer of correlations across a broadband XUV spectrum ($\sim 20$ eV bandwidth).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis neglects theoretically squeezed quantum phase fluctuations and residual technical noise compared to the shot-to-shot phase fluctuations.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup, the transfer of the four-lobed correlation structure from the IR to the XUV spectrum, and temporal reconstructions showing suppressed fluctuations in the joint signal.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the challenge, then detailing the use of TMBSV perturbation on HHG, demonstrating the transfer of correlations via covariance measurements, and finally using even harmonics and joint temporal reconstruction to confirm attosecond-scale phase-sensitive measurements.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Correlations between optical modes, ranging from classical fluctuations to quantum entanglement, are a cornerstone of modern optics and emerging quantum technologies. However, probing these correlations on the natural timescale of electronic motion - the attosecond regime - remains a major challenge. Here, we generate and characterize correlated attosecond extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission by perturbing gas-phase high-harmonic generation with two-mode bright squeezed vacuum. The signal and idler fields imprint their correlated amplitude and phase fluctuations onto two families of harmonics, thereby transferring these correlations from the infrared to broadband XUV modes. Even harmonics serve as an intrinsic attosecond phase-sensitive probe of these correlations through interference between indistinguishable XUV pathways. Shot-resolved covariance measurements reveal the amplitude correlations, while even-harmonics resolve the phase correlations with sub-cycle precision. Time-domain reconstruction of the correlated emission reveals a transition from maximal fluctuations to near-silence within only 30 as. Whereas the signal and idler driven attosecond pulse trains exhibit excess fluctuations individually, their joint reconstruction shows strongly suppressed fluctuations, reflecting their shared correlations. These results establish a framework for generating and probing quantum correlations on attosecond timescales, opening the door to quantum attosecond science.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports the successful demonstration of a high-speed, low-noise balanced homodyne detector by co-integrating a CMOS capacitive-feedback TIA with a silicon photonic chip. The resulting system achieves excellent performance metrics, including a 7.6 GHz bandwidth and 27 dB shot noise clearance. This integration proves the viability of CMOS technology for demanding quantum optical sensing applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly integrated, low-power platform for quantum optics measurements, directly addressing the hardware requirements for continuous-variable quantum key distribution and quantum sensing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core challenge is detecting and processing extremely weak optical signals, necessary for quantum measurements, while maintaining performance near the quantum-noise limit.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrated a high-performance, low-noise balanced homodyne detector achieving a 7.6 GHz 3-dB bandwidth and a maximum shot noise clearance of 27 dB.

**Method.** The system integrates a capacitive-feedback transimpedance amplifier (TIA) fabricated in 28 nm CMOS directly with a silicon photonic integrated circuit (PIC).

**Model / system.** The physical system is a Balanced Homodyne Detector (BHD) utilizing a PIC on the iSiPP200 platform and a CMOS TIA. The TIA employs a capacitive-feedback topology to minimize resistor thermal noise.

**Key observables.** 3-dB bandwidth (7.6 GHz), maximum shot noise clearance (27 dB), shot noise-limited bandwidth (13.7 GHz), and Common-Mode Rejection Ratio (up to 54.8 dB).

**Important parameters / regimes.** 28 nm CMOS technology, iSiPP200 silicon photonics platform, and the capacitive-feedback TIA topology.

**Assumptions / limitations.** Analytical noise models assume simplifications like C2 >> C1 and A0 >> 1; the system also faces limitations from PD quantum efficiency and fabrication tolerances.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the BHD schematic, the TIA topology, noise analysis comparing analytical and simulated noise, and measured performance metrics like output noise PSD and CMRR vs. frequency.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the co-design approach, analyzes the TIA noise sources and compares feedback topologies, presents the BHD characterization via S-parameter and noise measurements, and concludes with a summary of the achieved high-performance metrics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

A low-noise, high-speed balanced homodyne detector is demonstrated, combining a capacitive-feedback transimpedance amplifier implemented in 28 nm CMOS with a custom photonic integrated circuit fabricated in imec's iSiPP200 silicon photonics platform. The receiver achieves a 3-dB bandwidth of 7.6 GHz, a maximum shot noise clearance of 27 dB, a shot noise-limited bandwidth of 13.7 GHz and a common-mode rejection ratio up to 54.8 dB. These results demonstrate the suitability of CMOS capacitive-feedback transimpedance amplifiers for demanding quantum and coherent sensing optical applications, including continuous-variable quantum key distribution, quantum random number generation, and optical coherence tomography.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces and validates a scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-IR (sQFTIR) microspectrometer. By using quantum sensing with correlated photon pairs, it achieves rapid, shot-noise-limited spectral measurements. The technique is demonstrated to be highly effective for non-destructive chemical analysis of diverse materials, including pharmaceuticals and security features.

**Why it may be interesting.** The core physics relies heavily on quantum optics, specifically nonlinear frequency conversion (SPDC) and quantum sensing principles, making it highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** Developing a novel, rapid, and sensitive technique for chemical characterization and analysis of solids and interfaces using mid-infrared (mid-IR) spectroscopy.

**Main result.** The custom-built scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-IR (sQFTIR) system successfully demonstrated hyperspectral imaging of pharmaceuticals, banknote security features, and polymer identification through turbid media.

**Method.** The technique utilizes quantum infrared spectroscopy based on nonlinear interferometry, employing correlated photon pairs generated via SPDC to achieve spectral-domain acquisition without mechanical scanning.

**Model / system.** The system is a sQFTIR microspectrometer using a double-pass configuration with a periodically poled nonlinear crystal (ppKTP). It measures the interference of joint generation probabilities to infer the mid-IR spectrum from near-IR signal photons.

**Key observables.** Absorbance spectra in the functional group region ($3000 	ext{ cm}^{-1} – 2400 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$), fringe visibility, and spectral images.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Measurement speed of 100 ms, spectral range of $3000 	ext{ cm}^{-1} – 2400 	ext{ cm}^{-1}$, and spatial resolution on the tens-of-micrometer scale.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The technique assumes operation in the low-gain regime where difference frequency generation can be neglected.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup (Michelson-type interferometer) and show hyperspectral imaging results for dried insulin on gold, a banknote security feature, and polymer identification through a turbid ceramic medium.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the underlying quantum principles of the sQFTIR setup, describes the spectral-domain acquisition and Fourier transform processing, and then demonstrates the technique's capabilities through multiple applied examples.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum infrared (IR) spectroscopy is a novel technique based on nonlinear interferometry and quantum sensing with undetected photons. In this approach, spectrally far-separated correlated photon pairs are used for detection and probing, respectively. Hence, the probing wavelength domain (mid-IR) is substantially different from the detection spectral range (near-IR), which enables shot-noise-limited and cost-effective sensing schemes attractive for applied metrology. In this paper, we implement and employ a custom-built scanless quantum Fourier-transform mid-IR (sQFTIR) microspectrometer for chemical characterization and analysis of solids and interfaces. The sQFTIR system employs spectral-domain acquisition, without the need to scan the optical delay. This results in enhanced sensitivity and short measurement times and therefore enables rapid spectral acquisitions in 100~ms spanning a spectral band from 3000 cm$^{-1}$ - 2400 cm$^{-1}$. The capabilities of our approach are demonstrated for hyperspectral mid-IR imaging of dried pharmaceuticals (insulin on a gold surface) and investigation of a security feature on a banknote. Furthermore, we demonstrate hyperspectral imaging and spectroscopy through a turbid ceramic medium.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper presents an experimental method to certify multipartite Bell correlations in large quantum systems by employing few-body symmetric correlation witnesses. By using only two- and four-body correlators, the technique overcomes the experimental difficulty associated with measuring full-body correlations as system size increases. The results confirm that this approach is robust and highly sensitive, demonstrating a scalable path for quantum verification.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, experimentally accessible protocol for verifying non-classical correlations in large quantum systems by reducing the measurement burden from full-body to few-body correlations, which is highly relevant for quantum optics and quantum information.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the experimental challenge of certifying multipartite Bell correlations in large quantum systems, where conventional methods relying on full-body correlations become experimentally intractable.

**Main result.** The authors demonstrate that Bell correlations can be certified using only few-body permutation-invariant (PI) correlations, significantly enhancing noise tolerance compared to using only two-body witnesses.

**Method.** They utilize Bell correlation witnesses based on few-body PI correlators, experimentally testing these witnesses on postselected Dicke states for six- and eight-photon systems.

**Model / system.** The experiments use multi-photon states, specifically six- and eight-photon postselected Dicke states, whose correlations are measured using polarization correlators.

**Key observables.** Bell violation factors (R), white-noise fraction tolerance ($p_c$), and measured fidelities (e.g., 0.933(4) for 6 photons).

**Important parameters / regimes.** System size (6 and 8 photons), correlation order (two-body and four-body), and noise tolerance thresholds.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The certification characterizes the postselected ensemble, not a loophole-free test, and assumes the measured correlators are representative of the underlying state.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental setup for Dicke state preparation and compare measured violation factors (R) for different witnesses ($I_1, I_2, I_T$) across varying fidelities and noise levels.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of large-scale Bell certification, develops the few-body PI witness formalism, presents experimental measurements on 6- and 8-photon Dicke states, and concludes by demonstrating the enhanced noise robustness of the four-body correlators.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Certifying Bell correlations in increasingly larger multipartite quantum systems is challenging because conventional Bell inequalities rely on many-body correlations, which become experimentally demanding to estimate as system size grows. Here we demonstrate that multipartite Bell correlations can be certified using few-body permutation-invariant (PI) correlations with a fixed maximal correlation order. We experimentally test few-body PI Bell correlation witnesses tailored for six- and eight-photon postselected Dicke states. The addition of a few four-body correlators is found to significantly enhance the noise tolerance compared with previously studied two-body witnesses: for instance, for six qubits, the selected witness tolerates a white-noise fraction of $p_c\approx0.301$, compared with $p_c\approx0.048$ for the best two-body PI inequality with the same two settings per party. For six and eight photons respectively, we observe violations of the witness bounds by $32$ and $8.9$ standard deviations, arising from postselected polarisation states with fidelities of $0.933(4)$ and $0.916(11)$ to the corresponding half-excitation Dicke states. The witnesses for the six- and eight-photon cases use the same symmetric two- and four-body correlators, just with different coefficients. These results demonstrate an experimentally accessible approach for certifying multipartite Bell correlations in larger systems without requiring full-body correlation measurements.

</details>
