**Summary.** This theoretical study examines how combining strong electronic correlations with Rashba spin-orbit coupling affects superconductivity in cuprate-like materials. Using the $t$-$J$-$U$ model, the authors pinpoint a correlation-driven topological superconducting state ($C=\pm 2$) that manifests alongside distinct metamagnetic transitions. The work highlights the necessity of correlation effects beyond mean-field theories to accurately map the phase diagram of such complex superconductors.

**Why it may be interesting.** The explicit inclusion of RSOC and its interaction with strong correlations provides a rich platform for studying topological superconductivity beyond standard BCS theory, which is relevant for understanding exotic superconducting phases in correlated materials.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the joint effects of electronic correlations and Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (RSOC) on superconducting pairing, focusing on emergent topological and metamagnetic transitions.

**Main result.** The authors identify a distinct $C = \pm 2$ Topological Superconducting (TSC) state driven specifically by electronic correlations, which is accompanied by discontinuous metamagnetic and Lifshitz transitions.

**Method.** The analysis employs the Statistically-Consistent Variational Approximation (SGA) applied to the $t$-$J$-$U$ model, analyzing phase diagrams and free-energy differences.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled using the $t$-$J$-$U$ Hamiltonian augmented with RSOC and a Zeeman field, applied to a square lattice structure relevant to cuprate superconductors.

**Key observables.** Chern number ($C$), SC order parameter components ($\Delta_d$, $\Delta_p$), magnetization, and the free-energy difference ($\Delta F$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** On-site Coulomb repulsion ($U$), RSOC magnitude ($V$), and Zeeman field ($h$) are varied across different doping regimes near half-filling.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the SGA approximation and restricts the variational space to maintain lattice translational symmetry, excluding long-range SDW or CDW orders.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of SC amplitudes, energy gaps, and magnetization as a function of band filling, showing hysteresis loops and transitions between different topological states ($C=\pm 4$ vs $C=\pm 2$).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the phase diagram by varying correlation strength ($U$) and doping, comparing results obtained from the $t$-$J$-$U$ model against simpler weak-coupling schemes (BdG) to isolate correlation-driven physics.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Unconventional superconductivity commonly emerges in systems characterized by strong electronic correlations, with layered copper-oxides serving as a canonical example. Observation of spin-momentum locking within Bi-family of the cuprates, compatible with the presence of non-negligible Rashba-type spin-orbit coupling (RSOC), calls for an investigation of the joint effects of electronic correlations and RSOC on pairing in copper-oxide and related superconductors. Employing statistically-consistent variational approximation (SGA), we carry out such an analysis by constructing the phase diagram for the case of square-lattice \textit{t-J-U} model incorporating RSOC. We also investigate the effects of time-reversal-symmetry breaking by Zeeman field, as well as characterize emergent topological superconducting (TSC) states. Chern number $C = \pm 4$ TSC is found in a broad regime of on-site Coulomb repulsion close to half-filling. The latter is not governed by correlations and emerges also within the weak-coupling Bogoliubov-de Gennes (BdG) scheme. Yet, we identify a distinct $C = \pm 2$ TSC state that is driven specifically by electronic correlations via a topological transition occurring with no bulk quasiparticle gap closure, and is accompanied by discontinuous metamagnetic and Lifshitz transitions. Moreover, a qualitatively distinct doping evolution of the $d$- and $p$-wave components of the underlying mixed-parity SC order parameter above the metal-to-insulator transition is demonstrated. Our work points toward the relevance of joint correlation and RSOC effects beyond BdG scheme to phase diagrams of RSOC-coupled superconductors.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proves that Shor's algorithm loses its exponential quantum advantage when subjected to even arbitrarily small amounts of depolarizing noise. By analyzing the measurement probability using the Pauli path integral, the authors show that the characteristic resonance peaks decay exponentially with the noise rate. This suggests that practical quantum computation requires error correction beyond the scope of the analyzed noise model.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a concrete, quantitative demonstration of how realistic noise models can fundamentally undermine the theoretical speedup of quantum algorithms, which is crucial for assessing near-term quantum hardware feasibility.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes how the exponential quantum advantage of Shor's algorithm breaks down when the quantum circuit is subjected to noise.

**Main result.** The presence of any small, non-zero depolarizing noise rate causes the measurement probability associated with the resonant peaks to decay exponentially, destroying the quantum advantage.

**Method.** The analysis uses the Pauli path integral expansion to calculate the measurement probability distribution in the presence of noise, comparing the noisy result to the noiseless ideal case.

**Model / system.** The model is Shor's quantum circuit used for factoring, specifically analyzing the effect of independent single-qubit depolarizing noise of rate $\lambda$ applied to the control register.

**Key observables.** The probability of measuring a specific bit-string $x$, denoted $P_\lambda(x)$, and the measurement rate within the resonance set $E_r$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The noise rate $\lambda$, the number of qubits $n$, and the Hamming weight $d$ of the Pauli word.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis is restricted to a single layer of depolarizing noise, and the conclusion does not rule out fault-tolerant quantum advantage.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the noiseless resonance peak probability using the Pauli path integral. It then derives the noisy probability $P_\lambda(x)$ and shows that the high-frequency terms decay as $(1-\lambda)^d$, while the low-frequency terms are bounded by $O(nd)/2^{n/2}$, leading to the conclusion that the total rate vanishes for $\lambda > 0$.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We argue that the exponential quantum advantage in Shor's algorithm is broken under one-layer depolarizing noise of arbitrary small error rate, by analyzing a resonance breaking phenomenon in noisy quantum circuits. First, we express the distribution of measurements on $n$-qubit strings as the superposition of the $4^n$ wave functions in the Pauli path integral. In the noiseless case, the bit-strings achieving resonant peaks guaranteed a constant rate of successful measurements to factor a large number. Secondly, when the middle layer of the quantum circuit has independent depolarizing noise of rate $λ$, for any Hamming weight $d$, we obtain corresponding measurement rate bounded by $2(1-λ)^d$ for higher frequency terms and by $O(n^d)/2^{n/2}$ for low frequency terms. The rate approaches to zero as $n$ and $d$ approaches to infinity. Resonance breaking destroys the exponential quantum advantage. Furthermore, we design a classical factoring algorithm in polynomial time $O(n^d)$ to substitute the low frequency contribution.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical paper develops a framework for 'commuting operator self-tests' to characterize quantum correlations. It applies this framework to a game based on entanglement embezzlement, proving that the optimal correlation is a unique self-test. Crucially, the result demonstrates a correlation that cannot be modeled by simple tensor products, advancing the understanding of quantum resource theories.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work pushes the boundaries of quantum information theory by using abstract operator algebra tools to classify quantum correlations, providing a rigorous mathematical tool (the self-test) to detect non-local quantum resources that defy simple tensor product descriptions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the characterization of quantum correlations, specifically focusing on determining when the optimal correlation for an entanglement embezzlement protocol can be uniquely described by a commuting operator self-test.

**Main result.** The optimal correlation for the entanglement embezzlement game ($G_{emb}$) is shown to be a commuting operator self-test that cannot be realized by any standard quantum tensor-product model, providing a novel example in the field.

**Method.** The analysis heavily employs advanced $C^*$-algebraic techniques, including the use of Cuntz algebras and abstract state characterizations, to prove the uniqueness and non-factorizability of the optimal quantum state.

**Model / system.** The model is a generalized two-player nonlocal game ($G_{emb}$) involving commuting measurements on a joint state, which is mathematically formalized using commuting operator correlations ($\mathcal{C}_{qc}$) within the framework of operator algebras.

**Key observables.** The optimal correlation $\hat{p}$ for the game $G_{emb}$, and the associated unique abstract state $f$ on the tensor product of local measurement algebras.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The structure of the local measurement algebras (related to $M_3(\mathbb{C})$ and $M_2(\mathbb{C})$) and the entanglement state $|\Phi_2angle$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The proof relies on advanced theorems from operator algebras, such as Harris' unique abstract state characterization and the properties of GNS representations.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from defining the commuting operator self-test framework, applying it to the specific entanglement embezzlement game $G_{emb}$, and culminating in the proof that the optimal correlation is a unique self-test lacking a tensor-product realization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that the optimal commuting operator correlation for a variant of Coladangelo's two-player generalized nonlocal game, based on the embezzlement of entanglement, is a commuting operator self-test. Our result gives the first correlation self-test for an exact entanglement embezzlement protocol in the commuting operator framework. Because the unique optimal correlation necessitates the exact embezzlement of entanglement, the correlation is unrealizable using quantum tensor-product models, even if the local spaces are allowed to be infinite dimensional. As such, our result provides an example of a commuting operator self-test where the Hilbert space shared by the two parties cannot be factored into a tensor-product of local spaces that is compatible with the local measurement operators. Our main proof technique relies on Harris' unique abstract state characterization of exact embezzlement of entanglement involving Cuntz algebras.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a method to classically verify quantum computations (BQP) using quantum self-testing techniques. It achieves a quasilinear resource bound by leveraging the LWE assumption and adapting protocols from the multi-prover setting to a single-prover setting. This advances the understanding of verifiable quantum computation in the circuit model.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on complexity theory, the rigorous analysis of quantum state verification and the use of advanced cryptographic tools like LWE make it highly relevant for understanding the physical limits of quantum information processing.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to construct the first argument system for BQP (Bounded-error Quantum Polynomial time) with quasilinear total resource requirements in the circuit model, enabling classical verification of quantum computation.

**Main result.** They achieve this by using computational self-testing based on the LWE assumption, resulting in a resource requirement of O(poly(λ, log g) * g) for a circuit with g gates.

**Method.** The approach combines computational self-testing, the LWE assumption, and the application of a compiler (Kalai et al.) to translate multi-prover nonlocal games into a single-prover argument system.

**Model / system.** The model is quantum computation realized through quantum circuits involving single-qubit Clifford observables ($\sigma_X, \sigma_Y, \sigma_Z$). The verification process is classical, relying on cryptographic assumptions.

**Key observables.** Winning probabilities ($p_{win}$), commutator norms ($\|[W_1, W_2]\|^2$), and the verification error rate.

**Important parameters / regimes.** LWE security parameter ($\lambda$), number of gates ($g$), and the error parameter ($\epsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumptions include the Learning with Errors (LWE) assumption and the sub-exponential hardness of LWE for non-uniform quantum adversaries.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates a compiled nonlocal game structure. Figure 3 shows the structure of a quantum circuit implementing a specific transformation.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds the argument system by first establishing a computational self-test for certifying quantum states, then using this test to dequantize efficient verification protocols, and finally applying a compiler to adapt the result from a multi-prover to a single-prover setting.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Computational self-testing gives a classical verifier command over the quantum register of a single computationally bounded prover. We use this framework to construct the first argument system for BQP with quasilinear total resource requirements in the circuit model. Our argument system is based on the learning with errors (LWE) assumption and requires total resources of $O(\mathrm{poly}(λ, \log g)\cdot g)$ for delegating a circuit with $g$ gates, where $λ$ is the LWE security parameter. This is achieved by constructing a new computational self-test for certifying the prover's quantum state and using it to dequantize the efficient verification protocol of Broadbent (ToC 2018). Specifically, this self-test enables the verifiable, random remote state preparation of tensor product states of the single-qubit Clifford observables $σ_X, σ_Y, σ_Z, (σ_Y-σ_X)/\sqrt{2}$ and $(σ_Y+σ_X)/\sqrt{2}$, with constant robustness: the verification error is independent of the number of prepared qubits. This approach was first proposed by Coladangelo et al. (ToC 2024) in the multi-prover setting. We replicate their result in the single-prover setting by applying the compiler proposed by Kalai et al. (STOC 2023)---which turns any nonlocal game into a single-prover argument system---to a modified version of their self-test.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes how quantum entanglement is limited in systems with long-range interactions by introducing the concept of 'collectivity.' It derives sharp upper bounds on entanglement entropy, showing that the scaling depends critically on the interaction decay exponent $\alpha$ relative to geometric thresholds. This work advances the understanding of quantum correlations beyond simple spatial locality arguments.

**Why it may be interesting.** The identification of 'collectivity' as a fundamental constraint mechanism provides a powerful, non-local tool for bounding entanglement, which is crucial for understanding quantum correlations in complex, interacting many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central problem is understanding the fundamental physical mechanisms that constrain the entanglement entropy in many-body quantum systems, especially when interactions are long-range.

**Main result.** The work establishes 'collectivity' as a mechanism, alongside spatial locality, that rigorously constrains entanglement scaling, yielding improved bounds (e.g., polylogarithmic) for regular bipartitions compared to arbitrary ones.

**Method.** The analysis combines rigorous spectral gap estimates, concentration inequalities on the one-site Schmidt spectrum, and a Mean-Field Renormalization Group (MFRG) construction for geometric cuts.

**Model / system.** The study analyzes generic gapped Hamiltonians on a D-dimensional lattice with Kac-normalized power-law interactions decaying as $r^{-\alpha}$. A fermionic pairing model is used to provide a concrete, solvable illustration of the general theory.

**Key observables.** Entanglement entropy ($S_A$), one-site Schmidt spectrum concentration ($q^*$), and the spectral gap ($\Delta$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The interaction decay exponent $\alpha$ relative to critical thresholds $D/2$ and $(D+1)/2$, and the lattice dimension $D$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The system is assumed to have a unique, normalized ground state with a finite spectral gap ($\Delta > 0$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the scaling of entanglement entropy ($S_A$) versus system size ($n$) for various $\alpha$ regimes, showing distinct transitions at $\alpha = D/2$ and $\alpha = (D+1)/2$.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes general bounds for arbitrary bipartitions using fluctuation analysis, then improves these bounds for regular codimension-one cuts using an MFRG approach, and finally confirms these results using a solvable quadratic fermionic model.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Understanding what limits many-body quantum entanglement is a central problem in physics. Spatial locality has long provided a fundamental mechanism: correlations between a region and its complement must be mediated through a small spatial interface, thereby constraining their entanglement. Here we show that universal constraints on entanglement can persist even when interactions are strongly nonlocal, through collectivity: many weak interactions suppress collective quantum fluctuations while retaining a finite overall interaction scale. We establish this mechanism rigorously for generic gapped Hamiltonians with Kac-normalized power-law interactions $r^{-α}$ on a $D$-dimensional lattice. For arbitrary bipartitions, we prove that the ground-state entanglement scales at most logarithmically with system size for $α<D/2$ and subextensively for $D/2<α<D$, due to suppressed collective fluctuations around individual sites. For spatially regular bipartitions with codimension-one boundaries, we show that collective suppression can be propagated to successively larger length scales through a renormalization-group construction. As a result, we prove that the entanglement bound improves to polylogarithmic scaling for $D/2<α<(D+1)/2$, and remains parametrically stronger than the arbitrary-bipartition bound for $(D+1)/2<α<D$. Together, these results reveal collectivity as a fundamental mechanism for constraining many-body entanglement alongside spatial locality.

</details>

**Summary.** This work extends the concept of device-independent quantum steering quantification to three parties, analyzing two distinct tripartite scenarios. By employing the Assemblage Moment Matrices framework, the authors construct Semidefinite Programs to derive lower bounds on steering robustness. This provides a powerful, experimentally verifiable tool for certifying genuine multipartite nonlocality.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous, device-independent quantification of multipartite entanglement measures like steering is fundamental for certifying genuine multipartite quantum correlations in experimental settings.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper extends the device-independent (DI) quantification of quantum steering from the bipartite to the tripartite setting, analyzing two specific configurations: 2-steer-1 and 1-steer-2.

**Main result.** They develop Semidefinite Programs (SDPs) that yield lower bounds on the steering robustness for both tripartite scenarios, confirming the DI certification of measurement incompatibility.

**Method.** The core method involves extending the Assemblage Moment Matrices (AMMs) framework to construct SDPs based on observed correlations or violations of Bell inequalities.

**Model / system.** The analysis concerns a tripartite quantum state shared by three parties (Alice, Bob, Charlie) and quantifies the non-local correlations captured by quantum steering.

**Key observables.** Steering Robustness (SR), correlations $P(a, b, c|x, y, z)$, and violations of Bell inequalities like Mermin and Svetlichny.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The scenarios are defined by which parties are jointly steering which other parties (2-steer-1 vs. 1-steer-2).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The quantification relies on the assumption that the observed correlations can be bounded by SDPs derived from the AMM framework, extending previous bipartite results.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the two tripartite steering scenarios: (a) 2-steer-1 (Alice and Bob steer Charlie) and (b) 1-steer-2 (Alice steers Bob and Charlie).

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically extends the AMM framework to the tripartite case, deriving SDPs for both 2-steer-1 and 1-steer-2, and establishing bounds on steering robustness by relating them to Bell inequality violations.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Quantum steering captures the ability of one party, through local measurements on a shared entangled state, to affect the conditional states held by distant parties in a way that admits no local explanation. Its device-independent (DI) quantification -- requiring no characterization of any state or measurement -- has been developed in the bipartite setting, notably through the framework of assemblage moment matrices (AMMs) [Phys. Rev. Lett. 116, 240401 (2016)], but has remained largely unexplored beyond it. Here, we extend the AMM framework to tripartite steering, covering both the scenario in which two parties jointly steer a third one (2-steer-1) and that in which a single party steers the remaining two (1-steer-2). For each scheme, we construct a semidefinite program that, from the observed correlations -- or merely from the violation of a Bell inequality -- yields lower bounds on the steering robustness of the underlying assemblage. As a by-product, our bounds also certify, in a DI manner, the incompatibility of the measurements performed by the steering parties.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper explores the mechanism by which global symmetries can appear in quantum gravity theories when averaging over an ensemble of possibilities. It uses advanced mathematical tools, like the Siegel-Weil formula applied to CFTs, to show that this averaging process yields symmetries that are otherwise absent. This work proposes a new conjecture linking symmetry breaking in mixed states to the structure of ensemble averages in holography.

**Why it may be interesting.** The concept of symmetry emergence via averaging is a powerful theoretical tool that connects concepts from condensed matter (topological order, symmetry breaking) to fundamental questions in quantum gravity and string theory.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates how global symmetries, generally believed absent in quantum gravity, can emerge when considering ensemble averages of quantum field theories.

**Main result.** Global symmetries emerge from the ensemble average calculation, which is mathematically realized by equating the average partition function to a specific Eisenstein series, suggesting a mechanism for symmetry emergence in holographic contexts.

**Method.** The core method involves computing ensemble averages of partition functions (theta functions) using the Siegel-Weil formula, relating them to sums over bulk geometries (Eisenstein series).

**Model / system.** The study uses 2D Narain-type CFTs whose ensemble average is dual to a 3D Abelian Chern-Simons theory in the context of holography. It also analyzes Strong-to-Weak Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking (SWSSB) in the thermofield-double construction.

**Key observables.** The ensemble average of the theta function $\langle \vartheta_{Q, \alpha} angle$, the R\'enyi-2 correlator, and the resulting Eisenstein series $E_{Q, \alpha}$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The quadratic form $Q(\ell)$, the moduli space $M_Q$, and the large-distance limit $|x-y| 	o \infty$ for correlation functions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the ensemble average resolves the 'factorization puzzle' in AdS/CFT, and it proposes a new Swampland conjecture based on these findings.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 illustrates the 'factorization puzzle,' contrasting factorized contributions from disconnected bulk geometries versus non-factorizing contributions from wormhole geometries, which the ensemble average is expected to resolve.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the problem of symmetry emergence in quantum gravity, to applying the Siegel-Weil formula to CFT ensembles, and finally generalizing the concept to recast SWSSB in holographic models.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

It is widely believed that there are no exact global symmetries in quantum gravity. We review recent works showing that global symmetries can nevertheless emerge after ensemble averages of theories, as encountered in holography. As a precision case study, we discuss the ensemble average of two-dimensional Narain-type conformal field theories associated with an even quadratic form of general signature, which is computed by the Siegel-Weil formula and interpreted as a sum over geometries in a three-dimensional Abelian Chern-Simons theory. Global symmetries of the bulk anyons can emerge after the average, as T-dualities relating different theories in the ensemble are "folded" into symmetries of a single theory (duality origami). We discuss the relation to the Swampland program, including the emergence of global symmetries at infinite distance. Finally, we recast strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking (SWSSB) of mixed states as an emergence of symmetries in ensemble averages; in holography, wormholes connecting the two sides of a thermofield-double construction provide its bulk realization. This motivates a new Swampland conjecture.

</details>

**Summary.** This work explores excitonic stripe order in the two-orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model, treating it as an excitonic analogue of charge/spin stripes. Using Hartree-Fock and RPA, the authors demonstrate that excitonic stripes form a distinct symmetry-broken state whose spin character depends critically on the Hund's coupling sign. The results provide a detailed phase diagram mapping out various correlated electronic phases.

**Why it may be interesting.** While focused on condensed matter, the study's rigorous use of symmetry analysis and mean-field techniques for identifying distinct symmetry-broken phases is relevant to understanding order parameters in complex quantum many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates excitonic stripe order, an excitonic analogue of stripe order, in a multi-orbital correlated electron system.

**Main result.** Excitonic stripes are established as a distinct symmetry-broken state in multi-orbital correlated systems, with the spin character (singlet vs. triplet) dictated by the sign of Hund's exchange coupling.

**Method.** The study employs unrestricted real-space Hartree-Fock calculations complemented by Random-Phase-Approximation (RPA) instability analysis to map out phase diagrams.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by the two-orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model on a square lattice. The Hamiltonian includes hopping, crystal-field splitting, and various repulsive/exchange interactions.

**Key observables.** Excitonic order, stripe order (spatial modulation of inter-orbital particle-hole coherence), and the spontaneous breaking of a relative orbital Z2 symmetry.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hund's exchange coupling (J_H), crystal-field splitting (Delta_cf), and doping level are key parameters controlling the resulting ordered phase.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on mean-field approximations (Hartree-Fock) and RPA, which are noted to be limited by the Mermin-Wagner theorem for true long-range order at finite temperature.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates principal ordered phases (Néel, orbital density wave, excitonic order) at the Hartree-Fock level. Figure 2 shows temperature-electron density phase diagrams for various regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the internal symmetries of the Hamiltonian, develops gap equations for different ordered phases (AFM, Triplet Excitonic, ODW, Singlet Excitonic), and uses RPA susceptibility calculations to determine instability boundaries.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Excitonic condensation and stripe formation are two distinct manifestations of electronic correlations. While excitonic order naturally arises in multi-orbital systems, stripe order is a prominent feature of doped correlated-electron models. Here, we investigate an excitonic analogue of stripe order in the two--orbital Hubbard-Kanamori model on the square lattice, characterized by a spatial modulation of inter-orbital particle-hole coherence and, in the orbital-parity-symmetric limit, spontaneous breaking of a relative orbital $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry. Using unrestricted real-space Hartree-Fock calculations complemented by random-phase-approximation instability analysis, we determine how the Kanamori interactions select different excitonic channels. The sign of Hund's exchange controls the spin character of the condensate: ferromagnetic Hund coupling favors triplet excitonic order, whereas antiferromagnetic Hund coupling stabilizes singlet excitonic order. Upon doping, commensurate excitonic density waves develop incommensurate textures, including excitonic stripes and, in the triplet sector, spiral excitonic density waves. We further show that crystal-field splitting strongly reorganizes the excitonic instability by modifying inter-orbital nesting and can stabilize triplet excitonic order even in the absence of pair hopping. Our results establish excitonic stripes as a distinct symmetry-broken state of multi-orbital correlated systems and identify microscopic routes for their stabilization.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper provides a comprehensive mathematical review of spin-$s$ chains whose interactions are governed by the singlet projection, leading to a Temperley-Lieb algebra structure. Key findings include determining the exact spectral gap and proving that the ground state projectors obey the Jones-Wenzl recursion. It advances the understanding of how symmetry breaking can occur in gapped quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The deep connection between quantum spin chains, Temperley-Lieb algebras, and spectral properties provides powerful mathematical tools applicable to understanding gap closing and critical behavior in many-body quantum systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper reviews and extends mathematical results concerning the energy spectrum of spin-$s$ quantum chains governed by nearest-neighbor interactions derived from the singlet projection.

**Main result.** The authors determine the exact spectral gap for the fully polarized state as $1 - 2/d$ and show that the ground state projectors satisfy the Jones-Wenzl recursion.

**Method.** The analysis combines algebraic techniques (Temperley-Lieb algebra), variational estimates, and finite-size criteria (Knabe's criterion) to analyze the spectral properties.

**Model / system.** The model is a spin-$s$ chain with a nearest neighbor interaction proportional to the projection onto the singlet state of two spin-$s$ degrees of freedom. This interaction generates a Temperley-Lieb algebra with loop parameter $d=2s+1$.

**Key observables.** Spectral gap, ground state degeneracy (quantum integers $[L+1]_q$), and the ordering of energy levels across symmetry sectors.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Spin quantum number $s$, loop parameter $d=2s+1$, and the chain length $L$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the interaction terms generate a Temperley-Lieb algebra and utilizes established results regarding the structure of the Hamiltonian.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically reviews the model's algebraic structure, proves ferromagnetic ordering of energy levels, calculates the spectral gap using variational methods, analyzes open chain ground states via the Jones-Wenzl recursion, and concludes by discussing symmetry breaking.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We review mathematical results about the spectrum of spin-$s$ chains with a nearest neighbor interaction given by the projection onto the singlet state of two spin-$s$ degrees of freedom. Up to normalization, these interaction terms generate a Temperley-Lieb algebra at loop parameter $d=2s+1$. We also present several new results. First, we prove a ferromagnetic ordering of energy levels across symmetry sectors of the model, thus generalizing a previous result of Nachtergaele, Spitzer and Starr (2004) for the spin-$\tfrac12$ $XXZ$ chain. This enables us to determine a uniform lower bound on the finite volume spectral gap for these spin chains. By combining a variational estimate with Knabe's finite size criterion, we show that the exact spectral gap of the GNS Hamiltonian of the fully polarized state is $1-2/d$. Furthermore, this value serves as a lower bound for the gap of the maximally mixed ground state. Finally, we show that the ground state projectors on open chains satisfy the Jones-Wenzl recursion, thereby recovering a known result that the degeneracies are the quantum integers $[L+1]_q$ for $q+q^{-1}=d$. We discuss how the high degeneracy of the ground states allows the model to break a continuous symmetry while remaining gapped, and renders that gap unstable.

</details>

**Summary.** This work characterizes the structure of quantum Gibbs states in 1D systems, showing they are highly structured and can be prepared efficiently using only constant-depth quantum circuits. The findings establish strong bounds on entanglement, demonstrating that long-range localizable entanglement vanishes rapidly in 1D at finite temperatures. This has significant implications for understanding quantum thermalization dynamics.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous, resource-theoretic bounds on the entanglement structure of thermal states, which is crucial for understanding how quantum information is stored and processed in realistic, interacting many-body systems.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the structural properties and resource requirements for preparing quantum Gibbs states at thermal equilibrium in one-dimensional systems.

**Main result.** It proves that 1D Gibbs states can be decomposed into mixtures of product states over bounded blocks, allowing preparation via quantum circuits of constant depth.

**Method.** The authors use mathematical decomposition techniques, relating the Gibbs state to local operators and employing concepts from entanglement theory to establish separability bounds.

**Model / system.** The focus is on 1D spin chains (qubits) and fermionic systems governed by geometrically local Hamiltonians, analyzed at constant positive temperatures.

**Key observables.** Entanglement depth, entanglement width, localizable entanglement, and circuit depth complexity.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Constant temperature ($eta$ fixed), 1D geometry, and the constant depth bound $C_eta$ which depends on $eta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The Hamiltonian is geometrically local, and the results are proven for constant positive temperatures.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 schematically illustrates the construction involving Entanglement Bulk Decomposition (EBD) and the factorization of the state operator $\Omega$ over local regions.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general decomposition of the Gibbs state (Theorem 1) to proving its preparation via constant-depth circuits (Corollary 1), analyzing entanglement bounds (Corollary 2), and extending these results to fermionic systems and quantum thermalization.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We prove that the Gibbs state of any spin chain can be exactly decomposed into a mixture of product states over contiguous blocks of qubits with bounded length, at any constant temperature. As a consequence, any such Gibbs state can be prepared by local unitary circuits of constant depth, with efficient classical preprocessing. We place strong limits on the spatial structure of thermal entanglement: both the entanglement depth and entanglement width (measures of multiparticle entanglement) are bounded by constants, while the localizable entanglement (the bipartite entanglement that can be generated with the aid of local measurements and classical communication) vanishes exactly beyond a constant threshold distance. Our result also has implications for quantum thermalization: for any translation-invariant spin-chain Hamiltonian with nondegenerate spectral gaps, typical low-complexity pure states drawn from a maximally entropic ensemble at any constant effective temperature become locally indistinguishable from the Gibbs state upon unitary evolution. Additionally, we obtain an analogous decomposition for fermionic systems: the Gibbs state of any 1D local fermionic Hamiltonian is exactly a mixture of constant-depth local fermionic circuits acting on Gaussian states.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously determines the optimal query complexity for testing quantum juntas, which are quantum operations restricted to acting on a small subset of qubits. By establishing matching upper and lower bounds, the authors prove that the required number of queries scales as $\Theta(k/(\epsilon^2 \log k))$ in the forward-only model. This work highlights the deep connection between quantum verification tasks and classical combinatorial testing problems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection drawn between quantum junta testing and classical support-size testing provides a powerful theoretical tool for understanding the fundamental limitations of quantum verification protocols.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper determines the optimal query complexity required to test whether an unknown quantum operation (unitary or channel) acts nontrivially on at most $k$ qubits (a $k$-junta).

**Main result.** For the forward-only model, the optimal query complexity for both unitary and channel junta testing is established to be $\Theta(k/(\epsilon^2 \log k))$ for constant $\epsilon$.

**Method.** The authors establish the bounds by reducing quantum junta testing to classical support-size testing, using moment-matching techniques and Chebyshev polynomials to derive matching upper and lower bounds.

**Model / system.** The system involves an unknown $n$-qubit unitary or quantum channel $\mathcal{E}$. The testing is performed in a forward-only model, meaning the tester only has access to the operation itself, not its inverse.

**Key observables.** Query complexity, total variation distance (dTV), and the support size of the operation's action ($k$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Junta size $k$, distance parameter $\epsilon$, and the number of qubits $n$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The results hold for sufficiently large $k$ and $n \ge 2k$. The lower bound relies on the ability to exactly classicalize forward quantum queries on average.

**Figures summary.** Table 1 summarizes the query complexity for testing $k$-juntas across various settings (Boolean, Unitary, Channel) comparing classical, quantum, and inverse-free quantum testing.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the problem setup and then develops the upper bounds using nonadaptive testers. The core of the work involves deriving the lower bounds by reducing classical support-size testing to quantum junta testing, culminating in the matching complexity results.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We study the query complexity of testing quantum juntas. Given an unknown $n$-qubit unitary or quantum channel, the goal is to decide whether it acts nontrivially on at most $k$ qubits or is $\varepsilon$-far from every such operation. For unitaries, we consider the forward-only model, where the tester has access to $U$, but not to $U^\dagger$ or controlled-$U$. We give tight bounds for both unitary and channel junta testing. For sufficiently large $k$, $n \ge 2k$, and a broad range of $\varepsilon$, both problems have query complexity $Θ\left(k/(\varepsilon^2\log k)\right)$. Our upper bounds are achieved by simple nonadaptive testers using product inputs and single-qubit measurements. For junta channels, this closes the gap by Bao and Yao (COLT 23, TPAMI 2025) between an $\widetilde{O}(k)$ upper bound and a $\widetildeΩ(\sqrt{k})$ lower bound at constant $\varepsilon$, establishing the optimal $Θ(k/\log k)$ query complexity. At the heart of both bounds is a strong connection between quantum junta testing and classical support-size testing. For the upper bounds, we reduce quantum junta testing to a generalized support-size problem for distributions over random subsets, and develop a new tester with improved sample complexity. For the lower bounds, we proceed in the reverse direction, reducing classical support-size testing to quantum junta testing through a phase-masked hard ensemble and showing that forward quantum queries can be exactly classicalized on average. Together, these reductions identify support-size testing as the classical core of quantum junta testing and yield matching lower bounds. At constant $\varepsilon$, they also give a separation between $Θ(k/\log k)$ forward queries and $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{k})$ queries with inverse access.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces an optimized framework for randomized Hamiltonian simulation by shifting the focus from worst-case to average-case error analysis. It shows that sampling terms proportional to their Hilbert-Schmidt norms, especially when grouping commuting Pauli terms, yields significantly tighter error bounds than standard methods. This establishes average-error optimization as a superior, practical design principle for quantum simulation.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, theoretically grounded optimization principle (average-error minimization) for a crucial quantum algorithm (Hamiltonian simulation), directly impacting the feasibility and required circuit depth for simulating complex quantum dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper aims to develop optimized randomized Hamiltonian simulation techniques to accurately approximate the time evolution operator $U_t = e^{-itH}$ for quantum many-body systems.

**Main result.** By optimizing the sampling distribution based on minimizing Haar-averaged error bounds (using Hilbert-Schmidt norms), the authors achieve smaller error bounds than conventional methods like qDRIFT, with demonstrated improvements on large-scale Hamiltonians.

**Method.** The core method involves deriving nonasymptotic upper bounds for the Haar-averaged infidelity and signal error, comparing worst-case (operator norm) vs. average-case (Hilbert-Schmidt norm) error analysis.

**Model / system.** The simulations are applied to various quantum many-body systems, including the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev (SYK) model and molecular electronic-structure Hamiltonians, which are represented as sums of Pauli strings.

**Key observables.** Haar-averaged infidelity ($	ext{r}_p(t, N)$) and average time-evolution signal error ($\varepsilon_p(t, N)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The error bounds scale with $t^2/N$ and depend on the structure of the Hamiltonian terms (e.g., $	ext{Tr}(D_p)$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on deriving bounds for the mean time-evolution operator and assumes that optimizing the sampling distribution based on average error is a practical design principle.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares theoretical and numerical improvement factors ($	ext{IM}, 	ext{I}_r, 	ext{I}_{	ext{sig}}$) for both SYK and molecular Hamiltonians, showing that grouping terms leads to significant error reduction.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the general framework for randomized simulation, contrasting worst-case vs. average-case error analysis. It then derives nonasymptotic bounds for the average error, introducing the concept of grouping Pauli terms into blocks to improve the error parameter, and finally validates these improvements using numerical benchmarks on molecular Hamiltonians.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing. Randomized Hamiltonian simulation approximates the target dynamics by sampling quantum circuits and often allows simpler circuit implementations. We develop a framework for randomized Hamiltonian simulation in which Hamiltonian terms are sampled with arbitrary probabilities and the corresponding short-time evolutions are implemented sequentially. The leading channel error relative to ideal time evolution is governed by the variance of the sampled generators. Minimizing the variance-based upper bound on the worst-case error recovers qDRIFT, a leading randomized Hamiltonian simulation algorithm that samples terms in proportion to their operator norms. For typical input states, however, this sampling distribution need not be optimal. Minimizing Haar-averaged error bounds instead yields sampling probabilities proportional to the Hilbert-Schmidt norms of the terms. This choice can provide smaller average-error bounds than conventional qDRIFT. For Hamiltonians expressed as sums of Pauli strings, we combine this framework with commuting Pauli grouping to obtain smaller error bounds than conventional qDRIFT at fixed $R_z$ depth. Numerical benchmarks for the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model show error-bound improvement factors consistent with linear scaling in the number of qubits. For the 108-qubit FeMoco Hamiltonian, the error bounds are reduced by a factor of about 5.65. These results establish average-error optimization as a practical design principle for randomized Hamiltonian simulation.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces Parametric DRAG (PDRAG) to suppress leakage in superconducting qubit exchange gates. By controlling both the first and second derivatives of the pulse envelope, the technique significantly reduces unwanted leakage channels. This advancement is crucial for building reliable quantum processors by enabling high-fidelity gate operations.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a highly practical and numerically rigorous method for designing control pulses for superconducting qubits, directly addressing a major bottleneck (leakage) in realizing high-fidelity quantum gates.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is suppressing leakage pathways in superconducting qubits while maintaining the fidelity of fast quantum exchange gates.

**Main result.** The proposed Parametric DRAG (PDRAG) technique achieves significant leakage suppression, demonstrating geometric-mean reductions up to $5.27 	imes 10^5$ compared to base pulses.

**Method.** The method involves designing the pulse using derivative control (first and second derivatives) applied to the exchange interaction envelope, which is then calibrated to minimize leakage.

**Model / system.** The system is based on superconducting qubits modeled by weakly anharmonic transmons, described by a Duffing oscillator Hamiltonian. The control is implemented via frequency excursions.

**Key observables.** Leakage coefficients ($L_{11}$), gate fidelity ($L$, $1-F_{fSim}$), and the achieved suppression gain ($S$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Gate duration (12.5–35 ns), coupling strength ($g/2\pi=100$ MHz), and the derivative coefficients ($eta, \gamma$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the applicability of the rotating-wave approximation and relies on complex calibration procedures to tune derivative coefficients.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the construction of PDRAG, comparing leakage dynamics across different pulse protocols (Base vs. Calibrated PDRAG) and showing the spectral content of the control fields.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of leakage in fast gates, details the PDRAG method using derivative control, presents quantitative results showing massive leakage suppression across various gate times, and finally discusses transferring the optimized coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian model.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Programmable exchange interactions support quantum gates and many-body simulation in superconducting circuits. Fast excitation transfer, however, opens two leakage pathways in weakly anharmonic transmons, degrading gates and driving simulated dynamics outside the encoded state space. We introduce parametric derivative removal by adiabatic gate (PDRAG) to suppress both pathways while preserving the target exchange. Their conjugate structure determines first- and second-derivative corrections implemented through one real frequency command. At $g/2π=100$ MHz, calibrated PDRAG achieves a geometric-mean leakage reduction of $5.27\times10^5$ relative to the base pulse across 12.5--35 ns in Duffing simulations. At 13 ns, endpoint leakage reaches $1.98\times10^{-7}$ for the calibrated full-exchange pulse. Transferring the derivative coefficients to a charge Hamiltonian gives a mean 893-fold reduction over 12.5--22 ns after amplitude and carrier recalibration. Floquet return interference and charge-induced gap shifts explain the calibration and transfer gains, connecting compact pulse design to leakage-suppressed programmable interactions.

</details>

**Summary.** This work uses mu+SR to study how an implanted mu+ particle modifies the electronic state of localized f electrons in PrPb3. Key findings include observing quantized mu+ spin precession frequencies, which confirm a strong, anisotropic coupling between the mu+ spin and the Pr nuclear spins. This provides microscopic evidence of the interplay between interstitial impurities and localized magnetic moments.

**Why it may be interesting.** The observation of quantized spin dynamics and the detailed analysis of the spin Hamiltonian provide insights into strong local magnetic interactions and crystal field effects in rare-earth compounds, which are central to correlated electron physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the local magnetic effect of an implanted mu+ particle on localized f electrons in PrPb3, focusing on the interplay between the mu+ spin and the hyperfine-enhanced nuclear spin of nearest neighbor Pr ions.

**Main result.** Spontaneous mu+ spin precession with harmonic frequencies was observed for the first time in f electron compounds, indicating a quantized hyperfine field arising from coupling between the mu+ spin and the Pr nuclear spin.

**Method.** The research utilizes Positive Muon Spin Rotation and Relaxation (mu+SR) measurements to probe the local magnetic environment.

**Model / system.** The system is PrPb3 containing an interstitial mu+. The physics is modeled using a spin Hamiltonian incorporating hyperfine coupling terms (H_SI) that exhibit Ising-like anisotropy.

**Key observables.** Mu+ spin precession frequencies (f_i), Mu+ Knight shift (K), and the time evolution of the muon polarization P(t).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The hyperfine field (HF) at the mu+ site is found to be quantized, and the coupling constant a_J is estimated to be around 10^5 mK.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The mu+ influence is assumed to affect only the nearest neighbor Pr ions, and the analysis relies on fitting the muon relaxation function to a sum of cosine terms.

**Figures summary.** The notes mention fitting the muon polarization decay to a sum of cosine terms yielding five harmonic frequencies, and a linear fit of the fundamental frequency versus the measured K_parallel.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the physical system and the mu+SR technique, to developing the spin Hamiltonian describing the coupling, and finally presenting the key results showing quantized precession frequencies and the derived hyperfine field.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The local effect of an interstitial hydrogen-like particle on localized $f$ electrons was studied in PrPb$_3$ by means of $μ^+$ spin rotation and relaxation. Spontaneous $μ^+$ spin precession with harmonic frequencies was observed for the first time in $f$ electron compounds. We demonstrate that the signal is derived from a coupling between the $μ^+$ spin and the hyperfine-enhanced nuclear spin of nearest neighbor (nn) $^{141}$Pr with Ising-like anisotropy. The signal also suggests a marked suppression of spin dynamics of the nn $^{141}$Pr in comparison with that of the bulk $^{141}$Pr. These facts strongly indicate modification of the $f$ electronic state due to the interstitial charged particle.

</details>

**Authors:** Yimeng Cao, Ranyiliu Chen, Chengkai Zhu, Xin Wang

**Summary.** This work develops a rigorous framework to quantify the resource cost in optimal quantum symmetry testing. By deriving representation-theoretic bounds, the authors prove that achieving the best possible error rate often requires the system marginal to possess specific structural properties, such as high coherence or support restricted to certain sectors. This deepens the understanding of resource compatibility in quantum information tasks.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides rigorous mathematical tools (representation theory, error bounding) to quantify the fundamental resource costs associated with distinguishing quantum states based on underlying symmetries, which is crucial for quantum characterization tasks.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates whether optimal quantum symmetry testing can be achieved without utilizing the quantum resource inherently associated with the symmetry group.

**Main result.** The authors derive quantitative bounds showing that resource-free optimality is generally impossible, and they establish specific minimum coherence requirements for achieving the optimum in certain cases.

**Method.** The analysis uses representation theory, deriving a converse bound on the excess type-II error based on penalties related to suboptimal types and deviations in Schur profiles.

**Model / system.** The model involves testing a unitary $U$ belonging to a specific subgroup $G$ (like the diagonal torus or orthogonal subgroup) against the Haar measure on $U(d)$, using $m$-query parallel protocols.

**Key observables.** Type-I and Type-II error probabilities ($\alpha, eta$), system marginal ($ho$), and representation-theoretic scores ($h_m(\eta)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of queries ($m$), the dimension ($d$), and the coherence measure ($C_{	ext{rel}}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis often assumes zero type-I error ($\alpha=0$) to derive the lower bounds on the type-II error.

**Figures summary.** The notes reference tables detailing spectral phase-order bounds, exact scaled coefficients for different groups, and the structure of active Schur sectors for various query numbers.

**Paper structure.** The paper builds from establishing the general representation-theoretic converse bound, applying this to specific groups (torus, orthogonal, Clifford), and finally analyzing the resource requirements (coherence, number of queries) needed to approach the theoretical optimum.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Can a symmetry be tested optimally without using the quantum resource naturally associated with it? For parallel subgroup-versus-Haar testing, we derive a quantitative representation-theoretic converse for every protocol with zero type-I error: the excess type-II error is bounded below by the sum of two nonnegative penalties, one for weight on suboptimal subgroup types and one for deviations of within-type Schur profiles from their typewise extremal profiles. At optimality, both penalties vanish, yielding support and weight locking for every optimal system marginal. Disjointness of the resulting locked set and the free marginal set rules out resource-free optimality, whereas overlap alone does not establish attainability. For the diagonal torus in dimension $d\geq 2$, optimal testing without coherence is possible only with a single query. We determine both the exact optimal type-II error over all protocols with incoherent system marginals and the minimum system-marginal coherence required to attain the unrestricted optimum. For the orthogonal subgroup in dimension $d\geq 2$, a real protocol attains the optimum at every query number. For the qutrit Clifford group, Wigner-positive optimal protocols exist at three and four queries but not from five through nine; whether they exist beyond nine queries remains open. Together, these results relate the subgroup- and query-dependent resource requirements of optimal symmetry testing to structural constraints on optimal system marginals.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces SQUARE, a Structured Quantum Representation Adapter, which enhances frozen Language Models by mapping their low-dimensional bottleneck features through a parameterized quantum circuit. By measuring the resulting quantum state, SQUARE generates a structured feature map that explicitly models pairwise feature interactions. This approach achieves superior performance on downstream tasks compared to standard linear or low-rank adaptation methods.

**Why it may be interesting.** It demonstrates a concrete application of quantum circuit structure (parameterized quantum circuits) to enhance classical machine learning feature representation, providing a structured, physically motivated way to model high-order feature interactions.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses how to design a compact module to parameterize feature interactions within a low-dimensional bottleneck vector derived from frozen Language Models (LMs) for downstream tasks.

**Main result.** The proposed SQUARE adapter achieves state-of-the-art performance on controlled interaction tasks, significantly outperforming established classical and quantum-inspired baselines.

**Method.** SQUARE uses amplitude encoding of the bottleneck vector into a quantum state, applies a trainable parameterized quantum circuit, and measures the resulting state to generate a structured, quadratic feature map.

**Model / system.** The system involves adapting frozen Language Models (LMs) by projecting their fixed, low-dimensional bottleneck representation $\mathbf{z}$ through a quantum circuit structure. The circuit is parameterized and simulates the measurement of quantum expectation values.

**Key observables.** Average test accuracy (0.7565) on GLUE-derived tasks; basis-probability features and Pauli-Z readouts, which are shown to be quadratic forms of the input coordinates.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The bottleneck dimension $d$; the structure of the quantum circuit (e.g., RY-RZ-Ring-CNOT-RY); and the number of trainable circuit parameters $\theta$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The performance gain is attributed to the structured parameterization induced by the quantum circuit, not necessarily a claim of quantum computational advantage. The evaluation is performed on controlled interaction tasks derived from GLUE inputs.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares the feature map generation, showing the linear baseline versus the structured, quadratic feature map generated by SQUARE via amplitude encoding and circuit measurement.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the problem of feature interaction modeling for frozen LMs, proposes the quantum-based SQUARE adapter, details the quantum circuit mechanics and feature extraction, and validates its performance through extensive comparison against various classical and quantum-inspired baselines on controlled tasks.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Frozen language models (LMs) are increasingly used as fixed feature extractors for downstream reranking, scoring, and preference modeling, raising a practical question: how should a compact module represent interactions among features in a fixed low-dimensional bottleneck? Common linear and low-rank adapters remain linear at the adaptation module itself, whereas explicit second-order alternatives introduce pairwise interactions through direct parameterization or predefined factorizations. We propose SQUARE, a Structured QUAntum REpresentation adapter that amplitude-encodes the bottleneck vector, applies a parameterized quantum circuit, and measures the resulting state. We show that each basis-probability feature is exactly a normalized quadratic form in the bottleneck coordinates, while the additional Pauli-$Z$ readouts are signed linear combinations of these probabilities. The measured map can therefore parameterize interactions over $O(d^2)$ coordinate pairs through a small set of shared circuit parameters, where $d$ is the bottleneck dimension. It provides a structured parameterization within, rather than beyond, the classical normalized-quadratic feature class. In a disjoint same-pipeline evaluation over eight GLUE-derived controlled interaction tasks and five shared seeds, SQUARE achieves an average test accuracy of $0.7565$, compared with $0.7355$ for an affine normalized-quadratic predictor, $0.7271$ for the evaluated parameter-matched Givens mixing model, $0.6817$ for an MLP, and $0.6155$ for a frozen-circuit control. Under reduced supervision, it also shows consistent gains over the strongest evaluated classical comparator, with the same qualitative pattern across multiple frozen LM backbones. All circuit experiments use simulation, while the learned feature map can be evaluated exactly in batched PyTorch without quantum hardware.

</details>

**Summary.** This work provides a detailed mathematical analysis of how well approximate isometries of quantum states must resemble true symmetries (Wigner symmetries). It establishes strong, dimension-independent stability bounds for the cone of states but shows that the state space itself exhibits dimension-dependent instability in infinite dimensions. This has implications for quantifying the robustness of quantum operations.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous mathematical analysis of stability for quantum operations is fundamental to understanding the robustness of quantum information processing protocols against noise or imperfect measurements.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the Hyers-Ulam stability of approximate isometries acting on the cone of positive trace-class operators and the state space of quantum states.

**Main result.** It proves dimension-independent stability bounds for the cone in both the trace and Bures metrics, but demonstrates that stability fails in infinite dimensions and requires dimension-dependent moduli for the state space.

**Method.** The analysis uses functional analysis tools, comparing approximate isometries to exact Wigner symmetries (unitary/antiunitary conjugations) using both the trace and Bures metrics.

**Model / system.** The system involves quantum states, represented by positive trace-class operators on a complex Hilbert space, analyzed using the trace distance and Bures distance.

**Key observables.** Trace distance ($\|A-B\|_1$), Bures distance ($d_b$), and the deviation from a Wigner symmetry.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The approximation error $\varepsilon$, and the dimension $d$ of the Hilbert space.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The stability results rely on the assumption of surjectivity or $\delta$-surjectivity of the approximate isometry.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by establishing stability results for the cone (dimension-independent) and then tackling the state space, culminating in a proof of instability in infinite dimensions using specific constructions.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We prove dimension-independent Hyers-Ulam stability for surjective approximate isometries of the positive trace-class cone in both the trace and Bures metrics. Here $\varepsilon\geq0$ is a uniform upper bound on the additive error in preserving distances. Such an approximate isometry is uniformly approximated by a Wigner symmetry (a unitary or antiunitary conjugation), with error at most $9\varepsilon/2$ in the trace metric and $2\sqrt2\varepsilon$ in the Bures metric, even if it does not fix zero. For maps fixing zero, the trace bound improves to $3\varepsilon$ even under the hypothesis of $δ$-surjectivity, independently of $δ$. In infinite dimensions, we construct bijections of the full state space, including mixed states, whose distortions tend to zero in both metrics but which stay a fixed uniform distance from every Wigner symmetry. For state spaces, stability holds in each fixed finite dimension with a dimension-dependent modulus tending to zero as $\varepsilon\to0$, but no such modulus can be chosen independently of dimension.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a comprehensive theoretical framework to derive the Fokker-Planck equation from a discrete master equation by taking the continuum limit. It rigorously calculates the rate of entropy production and entropy flux for systems coupled to heat reservoirs or isolated systems. This provides a powerful tool for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in statistical mechanics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a rigorous, general framework for deriving non-equilibrium statistical mechanics equations (like the Fokker-Planck equation) directly from microscopic jump processes, which is crucial for understanding open quantum systems and thermalization dynamics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper derives the Fokker-Planck equation and rigorously calculates the associated rate of entropy production from the underlying master equation.

**Main result.** The derivation successfully yields the Fokker-Planck equation and provides explicit, thermodynamically consistent formulas for the entropy production rate ($P$) and entropy flux ($\Psi$).

**Method.** The core method involves taking the continuous space limit ($\epsilon 	o 0$) of a discrete master equation, allowing the transition from stochastic jump processes to continuous diffusion equations.

**Model / system.** The analysis models general stochastic motion, applicable to systems interacting with multiple heat reservoirs or isolated systems, using a state space $x$ (generalized to phase space).

**Key observables.** Probability density $ho(x)$, Entropy $S$, Entropy Production $P$, and Entropy Flux $\Psi$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The small parameter $\epsilon$ (related to the discretization spacing), temperature $T_i$, and the system Hamiltonian $H$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The derivation relies on the assumption that the time evolution of entropy can be decomposed as $dS/dt = P - \Psi$, and that certain integrated parts vanish during the limit process.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first defining the master equation for discrete states, then deriving the continuous Fokker-Planck equation in the limit $\epsilon 	o 0$. It subsequently analyzes the entropy balance, deriving expressions for $P$ and $\Psi$ for coupled systems and isolated systems, confirming thermodynamic consistency.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

We derive the Fokker-Planck equation and its entropy production from the master equation. To this end we consider a discrete space of states where the master equation is defined and appropriate transition rates are introduced. A transition rate has two parts, one of which is the ordinary term proportional to the inverse of the spacing and the other is inversely proportional to the square of the spacing corresponding to the variance of the independent stochastic variable. In the continuous space limit, we obtain the Fokker-Planck as well as the rate of entropy production and the flux of entropy. We also consider the case where the space of states is the phase space and discuss the equations appropriate for systems in contact with several heat reservoirs and for isolated systems.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a multiscale probabilistic framework to reconstruct complex weighted networks from incomplete, coarse-grained data. By ensuring the model's functional form is preserved during aggregation, the authors can transfer parameters calibrated at a macro-scale to infer fine-scale details. This method proves highly effective for analyzing real-world systems like international trade and industrial flows.

**Why it may be interesting.** While the application is in network science, the mathematical framework of parameter transfer and functional invariance across scales echoes concepts used in renormalization group theory or multiscale modeling in quantum many-body physics.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is reconstructing weighted networks when only coarse-grained (aggregated) data is available, which is problematic because the underlying process occurs at a finer scale.

**Main result.** The proposed multiscale reconstruction method successfully recovers the fine-scale binary structure with high accuracy, even when calibrated using information from much coarser aggregate layers.

**Method.** The authors use a multiscale model of weighted networks (wMSM) designed to be functionally invariant under coarse-graining, allowing parameters calibrated at an aggregate level to be transferred to finer levels without refitting.

**Model / system.** The method is tested on empirical weighted networks, specifically the International Trade Network (ITN) and the Dutch production network (DPN), where aggregation occurs geographically or sectorally.

**Key observables.** Precision, specificity, accuracy, maximum degree-error, relative error in link count, and various structural diagnostics (e.g., clustering coefficients).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The density parameter $\delta$ and the strength normalization parameter $ho$, which are calibrated at the observable aggregate layer.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The model assumes that the functional form of the link probability is preserved under coarse-graining, which is a key advantage over standard maximum-entropy methods.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the ultrametric aggregation process for the ITN and compare observed vs. reconstructed country-level weighted networks for a specific year (1993).

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the wMSM framework, details its functional invariance property, applies it to two distinct empirical networks (ITN and DPN), and rigorously benchmarks its performance against state-of-the-art methods across varying aggregation scales.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

Network reconstruction from partial information is usually performed at the same resolution level at which constraints are observable. This becomes problematic when only coarse-grained information is available, while the relevant process occurs at a finer scale. Here we employ the multiscale model of weighted networks introduced in a companion paper and turn it into a probabilistic framework for reconstructing weighted networks across arbitrary aggregation levels. The model is built to preserve its functional form under coarse-graining, so that global parameters calibrated on an observable aggregate layer can be transferred to finer layers without refitting. We test the method on two empirical systems with different aggregation mechanisms. In the International Trade Network, countries are aggregated into geographic macro-regions and the observed coarse-grained layer is used to infer the underlying country-level network. In the Dutch production network, sectoral flows are reconstructed across the hierarchical industrial classification, using coarser sectoral layers to infer finer ones. In both geographical and sectoral settings, we benchmark our genuinely multiscale reconstruction method against a state-of-the-art weighted reconstruction model calibrated directly at the target resolution, and therefore using additional information available at the same (finer) scale at which performance is evaluated. Remarkably, despite this informational disadvantage, our method recovers the fine-scale binary structure with high accuracy, improving precision, specificity, accuracy and maximum degree-error diagnostics, while remaining nearly equivalent in sensitivity.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes a quantum Otto engine, focusing on how non-Markovian thermalization affects its performance statistics. By moving beyond the standard Born-Markov approximation, the authors show that engineering the system's energy spectrum near a quantum critical point allows for the simultaneous enhancement of efficiency and power while reducing fluctuations. This suggests a new pathway for designing stable and highly efficient quantum energy devices.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a deep theoretical understanding of how non-Markovian quantum dynamics can enhance the performance metrics (efficiency, power) and stability (reduced variance) of fundamental thermodynamic engines, which is crucial for quantum energy technology.

<details markdown="1"><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the non-canonical effects on the statistical properties (average values and variances) of efficiency and power in a finite-time quantum Otto cycle, moving beyond the limitations of standard canonical thermalization assumptions.

**Main result.** The average efficiency and power can be simultaneously boosted while decreasing their variances by engineering the energy spectrum structure, particularly near a quantum critical point induced by a bound state formation.

**Method.** The authors use characteristic functions and detailed derivations of expectation values ($\langle W angle, \langle Q angle, \langle W^2 angle$) to compare exact non-Markovian results against the standard Born-Markov approximations.

**Model / system.** The model is a quantum Otto engine where the working substance is treated as a quantum harmonic oscillator coupled to hot and cold thermal baths. The dynamics are governed by master equations and quantum Langevin equations.

**Key observables.** Average efficiency ($\langle \eta angle$), average power ($\langle P angle$), and their respective variances ($\epsilon^2_\eta, \epsilon^2_P$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The energy spectrum structure, the proximity to a quantum critical point, and the coupling strength (non-Markovian vs. Born-Markov regime).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis explicitly contrasts the non-Markovian regime with the Born-Markov approximation, which is assumed to break down under strong coupling.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the quantum Otto cycle diagram, the energy spectrum showing bound states, and plots comparing fluctuation ($\epsilon^2$) and the trade-off relation between $\langle Pangle$, $\langle\etaangle$, and $\epsilon$ across different time scales.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by defining the system and cycle, deriving the necessary statistical tools (characteristic functions, expectation values), comparing exact non-Markovian results to the Born-Markov benchmark, and finally analyzing the optimal conditions near quantum criticality.

</details>

<details markdown="1"><summary>Abstract</summary>

The fast-developing quantum technology is propelling thermal machine, which lies at the heart of thermodynamics, into a new golden era. Being stochastic because of the non-negligible thermal and quantum fluctuations, the efficiency and power of a finite-time quantum heat engine exhibit a trade-off, preventing the simultaneous achievement of high power and high efficiency. Conventional studies treat the statistics of a heat engine by assuming canonical thermalization, which is valid only under weak-coupling conditions. We here investigate the noncanonical effect on the statistics of the efficiency and power for a finite-time quantum Otto cycle. It is revealed that their average values and variances are highly controllable by engineering the energy spectrum structure of the composite system consisting of the working substance and the bath. Near the quantum critical point induced by the formation of a bound state in the energy spectrum, the average efficiency and power can be boosted simultaneously, meanwhile, both of their variances are decreased. Deepening our understanding of the usefulness of quantum reservoir engineering in thermodynamics, our result lays the foundation for the realization of efficient and stable quantum energy devices.

</details>
